p.seg: In the past, gentlemen cultivated virtue and established conduct;
though their bodies perished, their names did not decay.
What was the reason for this?
It was learning.
Learning is that by which one clarifies the spirit, expands thought, harmonizes emotions, and orders one's nature;
it is the foremost task of the sage.
At the beginning of human existence,
people were benighted and unknowing,
like treasures in a dark room:
if one seeks them, they are not seen.
When the bright sun shines upon it,
then all things become distinct.
Learning is the bright sun of the mind.
Therefore, the former kings established offices of instruction
to oversee the teaching of the sons of the state.
They taught them the Six Virtues:
namely, wisdom, benevolence, sagacity, righteousness, centrality, and harmony.
They taught them the Six Conducts:
namely, filial piety, fraternal duty, harmony with kin, harmony with in-laws, trustworthiness, and compassion.
They taught them the Six Arts:
namely, rites, music, archery, charioteering, writing, and mathematics.
When these three teachings are complete, the Way of humanity is fulfilled.
Learning is like ornamentation.
If a vessel is not ornamented, it cannot be considered beautiful;
if a person does not learn, he cannot possess excellent virtue.
Having excellent virtue,
he can therefore order human relationships.
Being beautiful to behold,
it can therefore be presented to the spirits.
Thus, the *Book of Documents* says:
"When working on catalpa timber,
after diligently hewing and carving the plain wood,
one applies the vermilion paint."
Hearing the sound of the huángzhōng bell,
one then knows the pettiness of beating an earthen pot.
Seeing the pattern of the dragon robe,
one then knows the coarseness of wearing coarse cloth.
Experiencing the instruction of the schools,
one then knows the hardship of not learning.
Therefore, the learner is like one climbing a mountain:
with each move, he goes higher.
He is like one waking from sleep:
the longer it lasts, the more sufficient he becomes.
Looking back at the path he has come,
it is vast and distant.
If, because of its difficulty, he slackens,
he is mistaken and wrong!
The *Book of Songs* says:
"High is the mountain, I look up to it;
great is the road, I travel it."
This speaks of loving learning.
Leaning on a post and thinking of distant places
is not as good as walking quickly, which will surely get you there.
Raising your head and chasing after flight
is not as good as cultivating your wings, which will surely enable you to catch it.
Living in solitude and wishing for wisdom
is not as good as devoting yourself to learning, which will surely lead to attainment.
Therefore, the gentleman's mind does not idly wish;
he must seek learning.
His body does not move idly;
he must follow a teacher.
His words do not issue idly;
he must base them on broad knowledge.
Thus, his disposition harmonizes with others,
and his virtuous reputation continues unbroken.
Confucius said:
"Without learning,
how can one act?
Without thought,
how can one gain?
Young ones, strive in this;
then you may be called followers of a teacher."
Even if a horse has swift feet,
but is not trained to the carriage,
it is not a fine steed.
Even if a person has fine natural qualities,
but does not study the Way,
he is not a gentleman.
Therefore, the learner seeks to study the Way.
It is somewhat like painting colors:
once the dark and yellow hues are applied,
the pure white body is lost.
If it is worn and does not change,
who knows its original plainness?
Zǐxià said:
"Practicing daily,
then learning is not forgotten.
Exerting oneself,
then one's person does not fall.
Frequently hearing the great words of the world,
then one's will expands."
Therefore, the gentleman in his learning
is unceasing,
like the movement of Heaven above,
like the course of the sun and moon.
He toils diligently his whole life,
and only stops after death.
Thus, even if one has talent,
but lacks the will,
he still cannot accomplish his task.
Will is the teacher of learning;
talent is the disciple of learning.
The learner should not worry about his talent being insufficient,
but should worry about his will not being established.
Therefore, those who undertake it are countless,
but those who succeed are few.
Thus, the gentleman must establish his will.
The *Book of Changes* says:
"The gentleman uses this to strengthen himself without ceasing."
The completion of great music
does not depend on a single note.
The harmony of a fine meal
does not depend on a single flavor.
The virtue of a sage
does not depend on a single Way.
Therefore it is said:
Learning is that by which one synthesizes all the Ways.
All Ways are unified in one's own mind;
all words are harmonized by one's own mouth.
Thus, wherever they are applied,
in action, there is great success;
in stillness, there is advantage and constancy.
In silence, they establish images;
in speech, they form patterns.
Relating events from a thousand years ago,
it is as if sharing the same moment.
Discussing the customs of different lands,
it is as if being in the same room.
Considering the reasons for the hidden and the manifest,
it is as if seeing their true state.
Tracing the beginnings of order and chaos,
it is as if pointing to results already seen.
Therefore, the *Book of Songs* says:
"Learning accumulates brightness unto illumination."
This is what it means.
Thinking alone leads to stagnation and lack of penetration;
acting alone leads to hardship and lack of accomplishment.
The human mind must have illumination,
it must have awakening.
Like fire meeting wind, it blazes fiercely;
like water flowing downward, it moves swiftly.
Thus, Tàihào observed Heaven and Earth and drew the Eight Trigrams;
Suìrén examined the seasons and drilled for fire;
Emperor Xuān heard the phoenix's cry and tuned the pitch-pipes;
Cāngjié saw the tracks of birds and created writing.
These are examples of the great sages learning from the spiritual and drawing from the categories of things.
The worthy cannot learn from the distant,
so they learn from the near;
therefore, they take the sages as teachers.
In the past, when Yānyuān studied the sage,
he heard one and knew ten.
Zǐgòng heard one and knew two.
These are both cases of extending from the category one encounters,
and deepening thought to gain understanding.
Not only do the worthy learn from the sages;
the sages also learn from each other in succession.
Confucius learned from King Wén and King Wǔ;
King Wén and King Wǔ learned from Chéng Tāng;
Chéng Tāng learned from the Xià sovereigns;
the Xià sovereigns learned from Yáo and Shùn.
Therefore, the Six Classics are the books through which the sages learned from each other in succession.
Though the men have perished,
their Way still remains.
If learners of today diligently apply their minds to acquire it,
they too can reach clarity and achieve broad understanding.
For all learners, the great principles come first,
the names of things come later.
When the great principles are grasped, the names of things follow.
However, the broad learning of vulgar Confucians
strives for the names of things,
details of instruments and tools,
boasts of glosses and explanations,
picks apart chapters and sentences,
but cannot synthesize the ultimate meaning of the great principles to grasp the mind of the former kings.
This is no different from a court lady reciting the *Songs* or a palace attendant transmitting orders.
Thus, they cause learners to labor their thoughts yet not know the Way,
waste their days and months yet achieve no success.
Therefore, the gentleman must choose his teacher.
The establishment of exemplary conduct is what makes a gentleman.
In exemplary conduct, nothing takes precedence over rectifying one's appearance and being cautious in dignified demeanor.
Therefore, the former kings instituted rituals,
creating ceremonial caps and robes with colorful patterns to display them,
and jade pendants with tinkling huáng ornaments to give them sound,
desiring that they be revered,
desiring that they be dignified.
How can one be negligent and disrespectful?
One's appearance is the sign and outward manifestation of a person.
When the sign is correct,
then one's nature and emotions are well-ordered;
when one's nature and emotions are well-ordered,
then benevolence and righteousness are preserved;
when benevolence and righteousness are preserved,
then great virtue becomes evident;
when great virtue becomes evident,
then one can serve as an exemplar of conduct.
This is what is called a gentleman.
A gentleman may not possess a foot of land as a fief,
yet the myriad people revere him;
he may lack the authority of punishments and penalties,
yet the myriad people fear him;
he may have no music of flutes and pipes,
yet the myriad people delight in him;
he may have no rewards of titles and emoluments,
yet the myriad people cherish him.
The means by which he achieves this is one and the same.
Therefore, Confucius said:
"The gentleman is dignified but not fierce;
composed but not arrogant."
The Book of Songs says:
"Be reverent in your dignified demeanor,
for the people take you as their model."
If one lets his dignified demeanor fall into disarray,
allows his gaze to become vacant,
and neglects his speech,
yet hopes that the people will model themselves after him—
such a thing has never existed.
When there is no one to model oneself after,
then those who are disrespectful will arrive.
Petty men are all disrespectful,
yet they bring resentment upon others!
They worry about their own lowliness but do not understand the reason for it.
How lamentable!
Therefore, the Book of Documents says:
"Even the sage can become mad if he does not reflect;
even the madman can become a sage if he is able to reflect."
What human nature tends to neglect
lies in the subtle and hidden;
what human feelings tend to overlook
lies in solitude.
The subtle and hidden are the source of manifestation,
and solitude is the beginning of what is seen.
How can they be neglected?
How can they be overlooked?
Therefore, the gentleman reveres solitude and is cautious about the subtle and hidden.
Even when in seclusion,
ghosts and spirits cannot see his flaws.
The Book of Songs says:
"Closely set are the rabbit nets,
spread in the midst of the forest."
This refers to dwelling in solitude.
Furthermore, there are those who, even in dire straits, cannot be thrown into disorder—
King Chéng and Jìlù were such men.
In the past, when King Chéng was about to pass away,
he was dressed in his ceremonial robes and cap,
and only then did he issue the words of the "Gù Mìng" (Testamentary Charge).
Jìlù, encountering disorder,
tied his cap-strings and only then died in the calamity of the white blade.
Even in the distress of imminent death and the peril of the white blade,
they still did not forget reverence—
how much more so during leisurely feasts!
Therefore, the Book of Songs says:
"Where it is deep,
I cross by boat or raft;
where it is shallow,
I swim or wade."
This means one is sure to succeed.
A gentleman's mouth utters no frivolous or jesting words;
his words are sure to have restraint.
His person commits no frivolous or jesting actions;
his actions are sure to have measure.
His words having restraint,
his actions having measure,
therefore, even with his wives and concubines, he cannot be disrespectful;
even with his friends, he cannot be overly familiar.
Thus, without showing anger, his virtuous conduct is practiced within the women's quarters;
without giving admonitions, his influence transforms the local community.
The tradition says that when the great man rectifies himself, things are naturally rectified—
this is probably what it refers to.
If even an ordinary man living alone is like this,
how much more so one who attains his purpose and acts throughout the world!
Therefore, Emperor Táng Yáo, being sincere, respectful, capable, and yielding, shed his light upon the four quarters;
Chéng Tāng did not dare be idle or remiss, and thus possessed the nine regions;
King Wén, being reverent and fearful, created that central domain of Xià.
The Book of Changes says:
"In Guān (Contemplation), the ablution has been performed, but not the offering.
There is sincerity and solemn reverence."
This means those below contemplate and are transformed.
As for the causes of calamity and ruin,
they have disrespect and negligence as their steps.
Can one not be cautious!
In the past, Sòng Mǐn died by smashing his head on a chessboard;
Chén Líng met with disaster due to a jesting remark;
Yán Bǐng created rebellion through mutual abuse;
Zǐ Gōng brought about assassination because of tasting turtle meat.
Therefore, the gentleman is humble in his personal conduct,
yielding toward his opponents,
dignified toward his subordinates,
and reverent toward his superiors.
When these four are complete, resentment and blame do not arise,
and fortune and prosperity follow.
The Book of Songs says:
"Quietly reverent in your position,
associating with the upright.
The spirits, hearing this,
will grant you good fortune."
Therefore, in his interactions with others, the gentleman
is joyful but not disrespectful,
harmonious but not conforming;
he is fond of others but not flattering or deceitful,
studious but not practicing empty actions;
easy to be close to but difficult to flatter,
often critical but seldom at fault.
Thus, he never severs friendships,
nor does he betray companions.
The Book of Documents says:
"Be cautious at the beginning and reverent at the end,
so as not to be in distress."
Ritual
is of urgent importance to a person.
One can tread its path for a lifetime,
but cannot depart from it for a moment.
If one departs from it for a moment,
then negligent and disrespectful behavior arrives;
if one forgets it for a moment,
then negligent and disrespectful thoughts arise.
How much more impossible is it to begin and end without ritual!
Ritual is the guiding principle of reverence,
and reverence is the essential feeling of ritual.
Without reverence, one cannot practice ritual;
without ritual, one cannot regulate reverence.
The Way is not partially abandoned;
they depend on each other to be practiced.
Therefore, one who is able to fully embody reverence in following ritual
is called a complete person.
Transgression gives rise to disorder,
and disorder brings calamity upon oneself.
In the past, Duke Huì of Jìn, due to a disrespectful beginning, had no heir;
Duke Wén, through reverent commands, revived the state.
Xì Chōu, through arrogant feasting, hastened his demise;
Jì Quē, through reverence toward his wife, received official robes.
Zǐ Wéi, through the "Dà Míng" ode, revealed disorder;
Wěi Pí, through the "Jì Zuì" ode, preserved his emolument.
Liáng Xiāo, through the "Chún Bēn" ode, lost his family;
Zǐ Zhǎn, through the "Cǎo Chóng" ode, prospered his clan.
The gentleman perceives inauspicious virtue as being like that,
and sees auspicious virtue as being like this.
Therefore, when standing, he must be bent like a chiming stone;
when sitting, he must embrace the posture of holding a drum.
In turning round, he conforms to the compass;
in turning at an angle, he conforms to the square.
His gaze does not stray beyond the space between the fastenings of his sash;
his speech does not exceed the positions marked by the tablets.
His voice and breath can serve as a model,
his spirit and vitality can be admired,
his bowing and rising can be taken as authoritative,
his bowing and yielding can be esteemed.
In narrating and composing, he has method;
in movement and stillness, he has constancy.
Leading with ritual, he is not negligent;
therefore, he is the model for ten thousand men.
All human hearts possess the principles of the Way,
but in their application, they differ.
Some apply them to themselves,
others apply them to others.
Applying them to oneself is called attending to the root;
applying them to others is called approaching the branches.
When the noble person governs with them,
he first attends to the root;
thus virtue is established and resentment is few.
When the petty person governs with them,
he first approaches the branches;
thus achievement is ruined and enmity is many.
When Confucius compiled the *Spring and Autumn Annals*,
he was detailed regarding the internal and brief regarding the external,
strict with himself and lenient with others.
Therefore, regarding Lǔ,
even minor faults were necessarily recorded;
regarding the multitude of states,
only major faults were put to brush.
Now, one who sees others but does not see himself is called blind;
one who hears others but does not hear himself is called deaf;
one who considers others but does not consider himself is called benighted.
Therefore, clarity is none greater than seeing oneself;
acuteness is none greater than hearing oneself;
wisdom is none greater than considering oneself.
These three things—lifting them is very light,
practicing them is very near,
yet people do not know them.
Therefore, the wise lift very light matters to bear the weight of the world;
they walk very near paths to exhaust the distances of the world.
Thus, virtue becomes loftier and the foundation becomes firmer;
victories become more numerous and love becomes broader.
The *Yì* says:
"'Fù': Success.
Going out and coming in without haste.
Friends come, no blame."
Is this not what it means?
The noble person, regarding himself,
is never without caution.
If I have goodness,
I fear others may not yet approve of me.
If I have not goodness,
I fear others may not yet disapprove of me.
Seeing others' goodness,
I fear I may not be able to cultivate it.
Seeing others' not goodness,
I fear I must be like them.
Therefore, in his orientation toward the Way,
when resting, he sits at its corner;
when traveling, he rides as its third attendant.
Above, it hangs from his cap strings;
below, it is tied to his sash and pendants.
By day, he roams with it;
by night, he rests with it.
This is what the *Pán Míng* calls 'daily renewal.'
The *Yì* says:
"Daily renewal is called abundant virtue."
Confucius said:
"Disciples, exert yourselves!
Do not abandon yourselves,
lest others abandon you.
How much more so if you abandon yourselves?
Then others will distance themselves from you far indeed."
Therefore, the noble person does not grieve that his years will decline,
but worries that his will may grow weary.
He does not let the Way lie dormant,
nor let righteousness lodge overnight.
To speak but not act—
this is letting the Way lie dormant.
To act but not timely—
this is letting righteousness lodge overnight.
Now, if action differs from words,
the error of words
does not encompass wisdom.
If words differ from action,
the error of action
injures benevolence.
Therefore, the noble person's task is to act upon former words.
People's error lies in grieving for the dead,
not in loving the living;
in regretting the past,
not in being cautious of the future.
They delight in speaking of what is already so,
enjoy contending over accomplished affairs,
slack off today,
and are negligent in the coming days.
Thus proceeding until old age,
hence the affairs of the rustic
cannot overcome his regrets;
the regrets of the noble person
cannot overcome his affairs.
Confucius said to Zǐzhāng:
"Shī,
I wish to hear about that in order to correct this.
If I hear about that but do not use it to correct this,
what benefit is there in hearing, even if I hear?"
Therefore, the *Shū* cites Duke Mù's oath,
praising transformation.
The *Spring and Autumn Annals* records Wèi's Běigōng Kuò attacking Qín,
praising proper conduct.
Now, a pearl containing grit,
a fine jade harboring flaw—
this is their nature, and the skilled craftsman works them to purify their nature,
so they become as if originally pure.
Therefore, observing these two things once purified,
one knows that humane virtue can be refined.
The superior takes more,
the inferior takes less.
It lies with the person alone—
who can forbid me?
One who crosses by a small boat,
his person is safe;
one who moves by refining the great Way,
his enterprise is beautiful.
Therefore, the *Shī* says:
"Carve and polish their patterns,
their substance is gold and jade.
Diligent, diligent is our king,
governing the four quarters."
The ancients have said:
Brightness emerges from obscurity,
the manifest is born from the subtle.
Therefore, the frost on Sòng's well
foreshadowed the cold of Shēngzhèng;
the sprout of the yellow reed
presaged the heat of Dàzhōng;
affairs are also like this.
Therefore, the noble person cultivates virtue
beginning from the age of hairpins and tufts,
ending at the hunched back of old age,
starting on level plains,
completing on lofty peaks.
The *Yì* says:
"'Shēng': Supreme success.
Use it to see the great person,
do not worry.
Southward campaign, auspicious."
This means accumulating the small to reach the great.
The petty person acts in the morning and seeks completion by evening;
he bestows while sitting and expects return while standing;
he performs one day of good
and seeks a lifetime of praise.
If praise does not come,
he says:
"Goodness is of no benefit."
Then he doubts the sage's words,
turns his back on the former kings' teachings;
preserves his old methods,
follows his constant desires.
Thus, his person is disgraced, his name debased, and he cannot avoid being another's servant.
Confucius said:
"For what does the petty person seek longevity?
He cannot be good for a single day,
long in wickedness—
his wickedness is extreme."
Now, there are great delusions that people cannot recognize themselves:
abandoning what they have to think on what they lack,
abandoning the easy to seek the difficult.
One's person and family—these I possess;
governing them is truly easy,
yet one is unwilling to do it.
Others and the state—these I do not possess;
governing them is truly difficult,
yet one desires it.
Even if one says:
"I have a method,
I have a method,"
who would believe it?
Therefore, one with illness is not employed as a physician;
one with foul conduct is not employed to delineate laws—
because there is no proof.
Zǐsī said:
"If one can master his own heart,
what difficulty is there in mastering others?
If one cannot master his own heart,
how can he master others?"
Therefore, one foot of brocade
is enough to show its craftsmanship;
one ren of person
is enough to show his governance.
Thus, the noble person is cautious in his solitude.
The Way for humanity,
is simple and easy indeed.
Cultivating it
is not like mining gold or carving jade, which involves hardship and difficulty;
nor is it like seeking profit and managing gains, which entails clamorous competition and vexation.
It does not require summoning yet arrives;
it does not need seeking yet flourishes;
the four seasons silently accomplish it,
without speaking yet it is trustworthy;
its virtue matches heaven and earth,
its merit equals the four seasons,
its fame parallels the sun and moon.
This is why Yú Shùn and Dà Yǔ rose from commoners to the imperial throne,
shedding coarse cloth and donning embroidered robes.
Thus an ancient saying goes:
"With the preciousness of utmost virtue,
where can one go that is not fulfilled?
With the glory of utmost virtue,
where can one go that is not accomplished?"
Later gentlemen,
though they may not attain its practice,
shall still approach it, so it is said.
Lutes and zithers sound,
not ceasing their harmony for lack of listeners;
benevolence and righteousness are practiced,
not extinguishing their Way for lack of followers.
Thus when the strings snap, the notes perish;
when the body dies, benevolence and righteousness are abandoned.
Zēngzǐ said:
"The scholar's burden is heavy and the road is long,
taking benevolence as his own responsibility—
is this not heavy?
Only with death does it cease—
is this not long?"
If the road is not perilous,
then one cannot know the horse's excellence;
if the burden is not heavy,
then one cannot know a person's virtue.
The gentleman strengthens himself in what is weighty to obtain blessings;
the petty person daily rests in what is light to incur calamity.
Someone may say:
"Is this Way truly believable?"
The reply:
"Why should it not be believed?
In an orderly age,
those who do good receive blessings,
those who do evil incur calamity;
in a chaotic age,
those who do good do not receive blessings,
those who do evil do not incur calamity—
this is due to variable circumstances.
The wise do not doubt the constant Way because of variable circumstances,
thus they follow whence blessings come,
and guard against whence calamity arises.
Whether one encounters [favor] or not,
is not up to me,
but depends on the times."
To bestow good yet receive ill is called fate;
to bestow ill yet receive good is called fortune;
one simply holds fast to one's purpose.
The *Yì* says:
"The gentleman fulfills his purpose by according with fate."
Yet those who do good but do not obtain blessings are still many;
those who do evil but do not incur calamity are still few;
considering both,
how can one abandon the many and follow the few?
Zēngzǐ said:
"If a person loves goodness,
though blessings have not yet arrived,
calamity is far away;
if a person does not love goodness,
though calamity has not yet arrived,
blessings are far away."
Thus the *Shī* says:
"Gently blows the valley wind,
only the mountains stand lofty;
what tree does not die?
What grass does not wither?"
This means that even in the month when flourishing yang spreads virtue,
there are still plants and trees that wither and fall, contrary to the season—
how much more so with the retribution of human affairs!
Therefore, to neglect farming because of years of scarcity or abundance
is not the way of a good farmer;
to abandon goods because profits fluctuate
is not the way of a good merchant;
to alter the good path because actions bring fortune or calamity
is not the way of a good scholar.
The *Shī* says:
"Majestic and lofty,
like jade tablets and scepters,
with fine fame and fine reputation.
Affable and courteous gentlemen,
are the models for all regions."
Raising jade tablets and scepters to比喻 their virtue
emphasizes constancy.
Human virtue—
is it not like an empty vessel?
When the vessel is empty, things flow in;
when full, it stops.
Thus the gentleman constantly empties his mind and will,
maintains a respectful demeanor,
does not place his outstanding talent above others,
sees others as worthy,
and sees himself as inadequate.
Therefore, people are willing to advise him without weariness,
and instruct him without tiring.
The *Yì* says:
"The gentleman receives others with emptiness."
The *Shī* says:
"That beautiful person,
what shall I tell her?"
The gentleman, regarding the good Way,
if it is great, recognizes it greatly;
if small, recognizes it small.
Goodness, whether great or small,
is all stored in the heart,
and then raised up and practiced.
What I possess cannot be taken away,
and what I lack is taken from others;
thus merit often precedes others while others follow.
Therefore, talent and quick-wittedness surpassing others
are not truly precious;
broad learning and eloquence surpassing others
are not truly precious;
courage and decisiveness surpassing others
are not truly precious.
What the gentleman values is
moving toward goodness, fearing he cannot catch up,
and reforming evil, fearing any remains.
Thus Confucius said:
"The son of the Yán family,
he comes close, does he not!
If there is something not good,
he has never failed to know it;
knowing it,
he has never repeated it."
Evil is like illness:
attacking it makes one improve daily;
not attacking it makes it worsen daily.
Thus when gentlemen seek each other,
it is not only to promote goodness,
but also to attack evil.
If evil is not eliminated, goodness cannot flourish—
this is the natural Way.
The *Yì* says:
"In *Pǐ* (Stagnation), it is not for the proper person;
it is not beneficial for the gentleman's steadfastness.
The great departs, the small comes."
This means yin grows and yang diminishes.
The ancients have said:
Two things are difficult for people:
delighting in attacking one's own evil is difficult,
and telling others of their evil is difficult.
Only the gentleman can do what is difficult for himself,
and can achieve what is difficult for others to attain.
Even when able to do what is difficult,
he still fears raising others' minor evils
while overlooking his own major evils.
The gentleman worries about this.
Therefore, he reflects, repeats, probes, and examines,
until what the other harbors is exhausted,
and only then fully knows the weight of his own evil.
Once knowing the weight of his own evil,
if he cannot accept from others,
and further abandons himself,
how much more will he reject others!
Wine and food are what people love,
and when people meet, none fail to offer them;
they are not stingy with what they love
because the other delights in them.
If delight in loyal words surpassed that for wine and food,
would people not love them?
Thus loyal words do not emerge
because there are none who delight in them.
The *Shī* says:
"It is not that I cannot speak,
but why this fear and dread?"
The eyes can see far to the horizon,
but cannot see nearby their own corners;
the heart is likewise.
The gentleman truly knows the heart is like the eyes,
therefore he strives to use others as mirrors to observe gains and losses.
Thus his sight does not pass beyond the walls,
yet he sees the affairs of states;
his hearing does not pass beyond the threshold,
yet he hears of events a thousand *lǐ* away—
because he relies on others' ears and eyes.
When others' ears and eyes are fully used by me,
then my intelligence and discernment are unmatched under heaven.
This is called: others have one,
I have ten thousand;
others are blocked,
I am open.
Thus one knows its height cannot be made round,
its breadth cannot be made square.
The rituals of the former kings established that
the left historian recorded events,
the right historian recorded words,
the blind music master recited the *Book of Songs*,
the various officials offered admonitions and exhortations,
utensils bore inscriptions,
banquet mats carried warnings,
conduct was examined monthly,
and actions were reviewed yearly,
all to ensure self-correction and uprightness.
In the past, Duke Wǔ of Wèi, though over ninety years old,
still remained diligent day and night,
eager to hear teachings and guidance.
He commanded his ministers:
"Do not think me old and senile and abandon me;
you must admonish me morning and evening."
He also composed the poem "Yì" to warn himself.
The people of Wèi praised his virtue,
singing the "Qí Ào"
and calling him "wise and sagely."
All rulers who revived their states
acted no differently.
Thus, the *Book of Changes* says:
"The nobleman cultivates and reflects with fear and caution."
The foolish, however, oppose this principle,
believing themselves already benevolent, wise, divine, and enlightened.
Possessing these four qualities,
what need have they of others?
Thus, their crimes become glaring,
their foul virtue spreads far,
the common people are heartbroken,
and spirits resent and lament,
yet they remain unaware,
growing ever more complacent.
If someone admonishes them,
they say:
"These matters
merely arise from your own mind
and issue from your own mouth."
Then punishment, execution, disgrace, and calamity follow.
If they cannot avoid these,
they say:
"It is because our virtues differ,
and you do not understand my way.
How can you blame me?"
Thus, they mistake their own errors for correctness,
persisting in their initial mistakes,
until they face personal danger and state ruin—
truly lamentable indeed.
The *Book of Songs* says:
"I admonish you earnestly,
but you listen dismissively.
Not using it as instruction,
you instead turn it into mockery."
It is said that when Shùn lived in his village,
he did not give gifts to every household,
yet everyone praised him as good.
When Xiàng lived in his village,
he did not rob or plunder every household,
yet everyone denounced him as wicked.
From this, we see that
whether people are worthy or foolish,
they praise what is good
and criticize what is evil.
This is human nature—
not necessarily due to private affection
or private hatred.
If one's conduct does not earn praise
but instead invites criticism,
it is because one has not fully grasped the principle of goodness.
If one fully embodies the principle of goodness,
like Shùn,
even if others differ from Shùn,
who would dare criticize them?
Thus, it is said: "To ward off cold, nothing beats a heavy fur coat;
to stop criticism, nothing beats self-cultivation;
to relieve heat, nothing beats approaching ice."
How true this is!
Nothing is more valuable than having proof in matters;
nothing is more discardable than words without evidence.
Speaking may not bring benefit,
but silence brings no harm.
The coldness of water,
the heat of fire,
the hardness of metal and stone—
these things never speak,
yet everyone knows their nature,
for their truth is embodied in their form.
If the sincerity of my actions
were like these things,
who would doubt me?
Now, if I do not trust my own conduct
but resent others for not trusting me,
it is like teaching someone to catch ghosts and bind demons
and then resenting them for failing—
how utterly confused!
Confucius said:
"If you wish others to trust you,
then speak little and act steadfastly.
Acting steadfastly
leads to enduring practice;
enduring practice
makes affairs clear and evident;
when affairs are clear and evident,
none with eyes will fail to see,
none with ears will fail to hear.
How could this be falsified?"
Thus, deep roots yield lush branches and leaves;
long-standing conduct brings far-reaching reputation.
The *Book of Changes* says:
"Héng brings success.
No blame.
Favorable to perseverance."
This speaks of persisting long in the Way.
When Yīyǐn exiled Tàijiǎ,
and Zhǎn Jì covered a cold maiden,
the people of Shāng and Lǔ did not accuse them of impropriety or usurpation.
Why?
Because of their accumulated virtue over time.
Thus, if dye does not accumulate, people do not see the color;
if conduct does not accumulate, people do not trust the deeds.
Zǐsī said:
"When words are the same, trust depends on what preceded the words;
when commands are the same, transformation depends on what lies beyond the command."
Slanderous words
all arise from associations, cling to events, and exaggerate similarities.
Who says Mount Huà and Mount Dài are not high,
or the Jiāng and Hàn rivers are not long?
If the nobleman cultivates virtue,
making it high and long,
what worries remain?
Thus, seeking from oneself rather than others
is not mere self-reliance
but recognizing the abundance within.
Zǐsī said:
"Affairs name themselves;
sounds call themselves;
appearances display themselves;
things position themselves;
people govern themselves."
All originate from oneself.
Thus, blaming others is obstruction;
blaming oneself is clarity.
Clarity leads to knowing repentance;
obstruction leads to persisting in error.
Persisting in error drives relatives away;
knowing repentance draws even the distant close.
When the distant draw close, there is constant peace and joy;
when relatives depart, there is constant danger and fear.
Since the beginning of humanity,
it has never been otherwise.
King Zhòu of Yīn was the Son of Heaven yet was called "the solitary man,"
while Confucius was a commoner yet was called "the uncrowned king."
All cases are of this kind.
Thus, a skilled angler does not change the deep pool to chase fish;
a noble person does not leave his mat to pursue the Way.
Governing within the space of eight feet, his virtuous influence shines brightly.
The ancients sang:
"Look at that dark bird,
perching on the hill's slope;
the way of benevolence is near,
seek it not far away."
It is human nature to dislike slander,
yet one ultimately cannot avoid slander.
What is the reason for this?
It is not that one begrudges effort and does not stop it,
but that the method of stopping it is contrary.
Slander, by its very name,
the more you flee from it, the more it arrives;
the more you resist it, the more it comes;
the more you dispute it, the more it multiplies.
Understanding this,
then a noble person finds it not worth doing;
being ignorant of this,
then a petty person finds it not worth gaining.
Emperor Shùn repeatedly examined himself,
Yǔ bowed to forthright words—
these are examples of understanding this.
King Lì suffered execution,
Wú Qǐ was assassinated—
these are examples of being ignorant of this.
These individuals are all recorded by name in former registers,
their forms depicted in arranged portraits,
some serving as models for the age,
some as warnings for the age.
Can one not be cautious about this!
Master Zēng said:
"If someone speaks of my goodness,
I only fear they might hear of it;
if someone speaks of my faults,
I only fear that upon reflection they might see my shameful expression."
Thus, when a noble person accepts his faults,
it is not merely to adorn his words.
Sincerely arising from the center of his heart,
manifesting in his countenance and demeanor,
his love for virtue is deep,
and his correction of faults is swift.
Like chasing a rabbit,
fearing only that he might not catch it,
thus he advances in his endeavors and does not regress in his achievements.
The *Book of Songs* says:
"Look at those wagtails,
now flying, now calling.
I daily press forward,
and monthly go on a journey."
This speaks of tirelessly moving toward goodness.
To hear of one's faults and not correct them
is called losing one's mind;
to reflect on one's faults and not correct them
is called losing one's substance.
Those who lose their substance and mind
are where calamity and disorder reach.
A noble person avoids such.
The *Book of Zhou* says:
"Do not use water as a mirror,
but use other people as a mirror."
A mirror can be used to examine one's form;
words can be used to know one's virtue.
A petty person is ashamed that his face does not match Zǐdū's beauty;
a noble person is ashamed that his conduct does not equal Yáo and Shùn's.
Thus, petty people value clear mirrors,
while noble people value utmost words.
Utmost words—without worthy friends, one cannot obtain them.
Therefore, a noble person must seek worthy friends.
The *Book of Songs* says:
"Chopping wood, ding-ding;
birds cry, yīng-yīng.
Coming from the dark valley,
moving to the tall trees."
This speaks of the duty of friends,
which lies in earnest and direct guidance to ascend to the good path.
Thus, a noble person does not befriend those inferior to himself,
not because he shames them and exalts himself,
but because those inferior to himself require his support to stand.
If so, then having no leisure to support others,
who will assist me?
My downfall would be imminent!
Thus, if the embankment is low, the water will overflow;
if friends are wicked, one's own path will become deviant.
Therefore, a noble person is careful in choosing friends.
Confucius said:
"To dwell and gain worthy friends
is the next best thing to fortune."
Now, the worthy—their words are worth hearing,
their demeanor worth emulating,
their conduct worth modeling,
and moreover, they excel in commending others' virtues
and delight in pointing out others' faults.
They do not conceal like a shadow,
nor do they avoid speaking like an echo.
Thus, I stand in awe of them
as if a stern father were in the hall,
and spirits were in the chamber.
Even if I wished to do wrong,
how would I dare?
Therefore, those who seek improvement in their associations and travels
must draw near to what they revere and keep distant from what they take lightly.
The *Book of Songs* says:
"Do not discard your side boards,
strengthen your spokes.
Often check your driver,
so you do not lose your load."
This speaks of drawing close to the worthy and seeking help.
A gentleman must value his words.
Valuing his words elevates his person,
elevating his person gives weight to his Way,
giving weight to his Way is how he establishes his teaching.
If words are cheap, the person is debased;
if the person is debased, the Way is made light;
if the Way is made light, teaching is abandoned.
Therefore, a gentleman will not speak with someone who is not the right person;
if he does speak with someone,
he must do so according to that person's way.
With a farmer, he speaks of sowing and reaping;
with artisans, of skill and technique;
with merchants, of what is valuable and cheap;
with clerks and scribes, of official duties;
with high officials and scholars, of laws and regulations;
with Confucian scholars, of learning and scholarship.
Thus the *Yì* says:
"Keeping still his lips,
his words are orderly."
This means not missing the point and hitting the mean.
As for a father's kindness and a son's filial piety,
a mother-in-law's affection and a daughter-in-law's obedience,
an elder brother's friendliness and a younger brother's respect,
a husband's reverence and a wife's compliance,
friendship requiring trust,
teachers and elders requiring instruction—
officials consider and know these matters daily within their districts and neighborhoods.
Even with an ordinary person, one may proceed in an orderly manner and speak of these things;
this is acceptable.
But to go beyond this
is not acceptable.
Therefore, when a gentleman speaks with others,
he makes his words sufficient to convey what his knowledge and thoughts have reached,
and the matters sufficient to accord with what their nature and disposition find comfortable,
not exceeding their capacity and forcing or constraining them.
If he exceeds their capacity and forces or constrains them,
then they will become confused and stagnant,
and will consequently suspect the gentleman of deceiving them,
or else say he "lacks understanding."
This is not intentional.
To show the obscure to one whose understanding is limited
cannot illuminate him;
to tell the subtle to one whose hearing is narrow
cannot make him perceive;
this is what depends on natural endowment.
Even if one says there is no dispute,
what can be done about it?
Therefore, Confucius said:
"To be able to speak with someone and not speak with them is to lose the person;
to speak with someone when one should not speak with them is to waste words.
The wise lose neither the person
nor waste words."
Now, the gentleman's words
are what he values most;
even if offered the jade of Xiàhòu
or the team of four of Shāng Tāng,
he would not exchange them.
Now, to bestow them upon vulgar scholars,
thinking their will is deluded and they do not value listening,
is this not to disgrace oneself and harm the Way?
Therefore, when a gentleman is about to speak with someone about the source of the great root,
and discuss the ultimate nature of human nature and righteousness,
he must first measure their heart and will,
assess their capacity and measure,
observe their keenness of spirit,
examine their slackness and decline,
then initiate to observe their harmony,
guide to observe their compliance.
The signs of compliance and harmony are emitted in sounds,
manifested in sight and hearing,
displayed in facial expression,
and moved in bodily posture;
only then can one probe the obscure and advance far,
achieve clear observation and govern the subtle.
Thereupon, one opens and expands to reach them,
follows what comes to advance them,
carefully explains to enlighten them,
uses varied references to broaden them,
establishes standards to correct them,
and disentangles complications to order them.
Be swift but not hasty,
slow but not negligent,
varied but not entangled,
expansive but not unrestrained—
desiring that they attain it themselves.
Thus, Dà Yǔ was good at controlling water,
and the gentleman is good at guiding people;
guiding people must accord with their nature,
controlling water must accord with its tendency;
thus, the task is not ruined and words are not discarded.
Xún Qīng said:
"Only after one is reverent in ritual may one discuss with him the methods of the Way;
only after his words are compliant may one discuss with him the principles of the Way;
only after his expression is obedient may one discuss with him the ultimate of the Way."
"Do not argue with one who has a contentious spirit."
Confucius said:
"Only a gentleman can value his words
and value his expression;
can a petty man do so?"
Zhòngní and Xún Qīng understood this, one after the other.
A questioner said:
"Some who encompass the ultimate discourses of the highest sages
and penetrate the grand achievements of the great sages—
why do they like to argue with vulgar scholars?"
The reply:
"Because they think the vulgar scholars are certainly able to understand.
How to verify this?
If they had the music of metal, stone, silk, and bamboo,
they would not play it beside a deaf person;
if they had the patterns of mountains, dragons, flowers, and pheasants,
they would not display them before a blind person.
They know the deaf cannot hear,
they know the blind cannot see—
this is clear and distinct in their own minds.
Yet when it comes to vulgar scholars, they alone do not act thus—
because those who understand distinctions are not clear.
Why are they not clear?
The vulgar scholar's misleading of the enlightened man
is like the quail bird deceiving a child.
The nature of the quail bird is to be good at approaching people;
it does not fly high,
nor fast,
hopping about as if it could be caught,
but in the end it cannot be caught.
This is why the child wears out his knees and tires his feet without considering it wearisome.
When a vulgar scholar speaks with an enlightened man,
the enlightened man, though unwilling to accept it,
has no grounds to refuse;
yet there is praise,
there is agreement,
as if he could be awakened,
but in the end he cannot be awakened.
This is why the enlightened man dries his lips and exhausts his voice without giving up.
Such a person is indeed one who obscures enlightenment,
not one who is truly enlightened.
Though he can speak,
he is still just a vulgar scholar.
Not only in speech,
but also in action it is like this:
if he finds his proper place, he is honored and glorious;
if he loses his proper place, he is base and disgraced.
In the past, Cāngwú Bǐng married a beautiful wife
and gave her to his elder brother,
wishing to be yielding,
but it would have been better not to yield.
Wěishēng made an appointment with a woman by the water's edge;
the water rose violently, he did not leave and died,
wishing to be trustworthy,
but it would have been better not to be trustworthy.
In Yègōng's district,
a father stole a sheep and his son bore witness against him,
wishing to be upright,
but it would have been better not to be upright.
Chén Zhòngzǐ would not eat the food of his mother and elder brother,
and went out to live in Yùlíng,
wishing to be pure,
but it would have been better not to be pure.
Zōng Lǔ accepted Qí Bào's plot
and died in the calamity of Mèng Zhí,
wishing to be righteous,
but it would have been better not to be righteous.
Therefore, all ways are difficult to tread,
and even more difficult to apply correctly.
Thus, the gentleman is careful about himself, using this as a mirror for the future."
The rise of arts—
does it stem from the wisdom inherent in the people’s minds?
Do those who create arts do so with reason?
People are born with minds that perceive things,
perceive things and then desires arise,
desires arise and affairs multiply,
affairs multiply and none can bring order to them.
Therefore, the sages, drawing upon wisdom, created arts;
through arts they established order in affairs.
These two—wisdom and arts—are close at hand within oneself,
yet extend far outward to things.
Arts serve to manifest wisdom, adorn ability, unify affairs, and govern the multitude.
This is something the sages could not cease from doing.
Arts are that by which one accomplishes affairs and cultivates virtue;
virtue is that by which one follows the Dào and guides oneself.
Arts are the branches and leaves of virtue;
virtue is the root and trunk of a person.
These two things do not operate in isolation,
nor do they stand alone.
A tree without branches and leaves cannot enrich its root and trunk,
thus it is called blighted;
a person without arts cannot complete their virtue,
thus they are called uncultivated.
If one wishes to be a noble person (jūnzǐ),
one must combine both!
The former kings, desiring people to become noble persons,
established the office of Bǎoshì,
who oversaw the teaching of the six arts:
first, the five rites;
second, the six musics;
third, the five archeries;
fourth, the five charioteerings;
fifth, the six writings;
sixth, the nine calculations.
They taught the six demeanors:
first, the demeanor for sacrificial ceremonies;
second, the demeanor for receiving guests;
third, the demeanor for the court assembly;
fourth, the demeanor for mourning observances;
fifth, the demeanor for military campaigns;
sixth, the demeanor for chariots and horses.
The Dàxū kept the register of scholars,
who entered the school in spring to lodge and practice,
selecting and harmonizing the myriad dances;
in autumn, they arranged the school to harmonize voices,
reciting, chanting, discussing, and practicing,
without slackening in due season.
Thus the Shī says:
"Lush and luxuriant is the artemisia,
on that central slope;
having seen the noble person,
joyful and with proper demeanor."
Nurturing the multitude of talents with beauty—
is this not like people's relation to the arts?
Having cultivated their substance,
and added refinement to it,
when substance and refinement are both evident, then the form is complete;
when the form is complete, then one may ascend to the pure temple,
and present offerings to the kings and lords.
Therefore, the noble person does not establish themselves without benevolence,
does not act without righteousness,
does not govern without arts,
and is not dignified without proper demeanor.
When these four are without fault,
then the vessel of the sage and worthy is achieved.
The Yì says:
"Abundance is called the great enterprise."
Is this not referring to such a state?
The noble person is one whose inner and outer correspond and whose root and branches are measured.
Thus speech and appearance correspond to the heart,
and aspirations, arts, and abilities are measured by virtue and conduct.
Beauty resides within,
and flows through the four limbs;
pure and genuine within, substantial,
radiance and brilliance manifest outwardly.
Confucius said:
"The noble person is ashamed to have the robes but not the demeanor,
ashamed to have the demeanor but not the speech,
ashamed to have the speech but not the conduct."
Therefore, mountains that treasure jade
must have moist earth and trees;
persons of abundant virtue
must have numerous arts and refinements.
In the past, the Duke of Zhōu
once pondered deeply on this.
Confucius said, "For securing those above and governing the people,
nothing is better than rites";
"for transforming customs and changing habits,
nothing is better than music."
What resides in the six arts
makes manifest the minor details.
That is, arranging the baskets and stands,
setting out the vessels and meat boards,
holding the feather and flute,
striking the bells and chimes,
the rhythms of ascending, descending, hastening, and hovering,
bending, stretching, bowing, and looking up—
these are not the root of rites and music.
The root of rites and music
lies in their virtuous sound!
The Shī says:
"I have fine guests,
their virtuous sound is very clear.
They show the people not to be frivolous,
the noble person takes them as model and emulates them.
I have good wine,
the fine guests feast and revel."
This is what rites and music value.
Therefore, reverence, respect, integrity, and yielding are the disposition of the arts;
balance, harmony, peace, and uprightness are the substance of the arts;
alertness, diligence, and inexhaustibility are the flourish of the arts;
dignified demeanor, perfectly timely, is the adornment of the arts.
One who comprehends the disposition and substance of the multitude of arts
may discuss the Dào with them;
one who recognizes the flourish and adornment of the multitude of arts
may discuss affairs with them.
Affairs are the duties of the officials;
the Dào is the enterprise of the noble person.
The former kings' devaluation of the arts
was essentially a devaluation of the officials' duties.
When the noble person combines both, they become noble.
Therefore, Confucius said:
"Set your will upon the Dào,
base yourself upon virtue,
lean upon benevolence,
and wander in the arts."
Arts are the servants of the heart,
the voice of benevolence,
the image of righteousness.
Thus rites are to examine reverence,
music to deepen affection,
archery to balance the will,
charioteering to harmonize the heart,
writing to connect affairs,
calculation to order complexity.
When reverence is examined, the people are not disrespectful;
when affection is deepened, all living beings are pleased;
when the will is balanced, resentment and blame vanish;
when the heart is harmonious, discordant virtue becomes amiable;
when affairs are connected, laws and warnings are clear;
when complexity is ordered, things are not contradictory.
These six, though different,
lead to the same end;
their Dào is what the noble person masters,
their affairs are what the officials jointly perform.
This is the general principle of the arts.
What the vulgar scholars call disputation
is not disputation.
Calling what is not disputation 'disputation'
is because they have heard the name 'disputation',
but do not know the reality of disputation.
Thus they see it wrongly.
What the vulgar call disputation
is glibness of tongue.
Those glib of tongue
merely beautify their tone and breath,
multiply their phrases and expressions;
like a fierce wind arriving,
like a torrential rain gathering,
they do not discuss the nature of right and wrong,
do not recognize the principle of crooked and straight,
aiming only at endless talk,
striving only for certain victory.
Therefore, those of shallow understanding who love novelty,
seeing them act thus,
firmly consider it disputation.
They do not realize that those who are simple and reticent yet comprehend the Dào,
though their mouths may be bested, their hearts are not convinced.
Disputation seeks to convince people's hearts,
not to defeat their mouths.
Thus the word 'disputation' (biàn) means to distinguish,
to skillfully differentiate categories of affairs and clarify how to handle them,
not to mean sharp, rapid speech that overwhelms and covers others.
Therefore, the commentary says the Chūnqiū is subtle yet evident, tactful yet discriminating.
Thus, the speech of disputation must be concise to the extreme,
uncomplicated yet illuminating,
pace and rhythm responding appropriately,
not violating ritual teachings,
sufficient to correspond to each other.
It delights in exhausting others' words,
skillfully eliciting others' intentions,
causing discussants each to fully attain their wishes,
and with them reach understanding.
Its praise is without seeking fame,
its principles are not solely self-evident.
If it is like this, then it may be called disputation.
Therefore, there is speech that is clumsy yet discriminating,
and speech that is clever yet not discriminating.
The gentleman's debate
aims to clarify the principles of the great Way,
how could it be merely to win an argument in a single gathering!
The human mind's relation to right and wrong
is like the mouth's relation to flavors.
The mouth does not find food delicious only when seasoned by oneself
and unpalatable when seasoned by others.
Thus, the gentleman's relation to the Way
is the same whether in others or in oneself.
If the Way is attained,
then my heart rejoices;
why should I choose between others and myself?
If the Way is lost,
then my heart is displeased;
why should I favor this over that?
Therefore, in his discourse,
when he encounters what is right in others, he stops.
If he encounters what is right in others and still does not stop,
but speaks recklessly and argues arbitrarily,
then he is a petty person.
Even if his words are elegant,
how are they different from the magpie's fondness for chirping or the bell's clamorous noise?
Thus, Confucius said:
"The petty person considers slander and criticism as eloquence,
considers harshness and impatience as wisdom,
and considers disrespect as courage."
These are what the sage detests,
yet the petty person considers them admirable.
Is this not lamentable?
The reason why glib talkers can thrive in the world
is certainly due to causes.
Moreover, the glib talker's mind is sufficient to perceive trivial techniques,
his speech is sufficient to exhaust clever rhetoric,
his readiness is sufficient to respond to pointed questions,
and his ability to refute is sufficient to settle common doubts.
Yet he delights in speaking without weariness,
chattering incessantly.
Those who can classify categories and distinguish things are few,
while the foolish and benighted who lack understanding are many.
Who knows their errors?
This is why they remain useless yet are not discarded,
and are held in the lowest esteem yet are not abandoned.
The laws of the ancient kings decreed:
Those who split hairs to break the law, or confuse names and alter institutions
shall be executed;
those whose conduct is depraved and stubborn, whose speech is false and eloquent, who record the vile and are widely learned, or who follow what is wrong and gloss it over
shall also be executed;
because they mislead the masses and confuse the people,
thereby undermining and corrupting the ultimate Way.
Confucius said:
"Clever words confound virtue."
He detested what appears similar but is not truly so.
Someone asked:
"Among scholars, some are wise and exhaustively understand principles,
while others are pure and sincere in their conduct and aspirations.
These two cannot be combined in one person.
Which would the sage choose?"
The reply was:
"He would choose the wise.
The function of wisdom
is to enrich the people and increase benefits,
enabling all things to fully realize their utmost potential.
What makes the sage attainable
is not merely empty conduct,
but wisdom.
Fúxī created the Eight Trigrams,
and King Wén expanded their explanations.
These all exhaustively understood the divine and comprehended transformation.
How could they rely solely on good conduct?
The 'Xì' trigram image in the Yìjīng says, 'The great man uses continuing brightness to illuminate the four directions.'
Moreover, the great man is a sage.
The other trigram images all refer to the gentleman,
for the gentleman is one who comprehends the worthy.
Acute hearing and clear vision only the sage can fully attain;
those of great talent and broad understanding may possess them but cannot fully attain them.
The Shūjīng praises Táng Yáo,
listing 'reverence' and 'clarity' as foremost.
When Huāndōu recommended Gònggōng,
and the Four Peaks recommended Gǔn,
Yáo knew their conduct,
but the masses did not yet know to trust him.
If not for Yáo, the borderlands would have many vicious clans,
and the common people would long suffer distress.
Such is the achievement of wisdom.
Which would you follow?"
Someone said:
"Both are called worthy;
why then discuss them in terms of the sage?"
The reply was:
"The worthy are also thus.
In human conduct, nothing is greater than filial piety,
and nothing more illustrious than purity.
Zēng Shēn's filial piety
could not be surpassed even by Yú Shùn;
Yuán Xiàn's purity
could not be faulted even by Bóyí.
Yet they could not be ranked alongside Yóu and Xià in the four categories of conduct,
because their talent was inferior.
Zhòngní asked Zǐgòng:
'You and Huí—who is superior?'
Zǐgòng replied:
'How dare I compare myself to Huí?
Huí, hearing one point, understands ten;
I, hearing one point, understand two.'
Zǐgòng's conduct was far inferior to Yán Yuān's,
yet he did not admire his conduct;
he admired his ability to hear one and understand ten.
From this perspective,
it is outstanding talent that commands admiration.
Zhòngní also marveled at Yán Yuān's outstanding talent,
hence he said:
'Huí is not one who assists me;
he finds nothing in my words that does not delight him.'
Yán Yuān comprehended the sage's sentiments,
so there were no endlessly difficult explanations for him.
Thus, he alone gained the reputation for earnest diligence,
and became the foremost among the seventy disciples.
Although Zēng Shēn was genuinely filial
and Yuán Xiàn was inherently pure,
Zhòngní did not greatly praise them."
Someone asked:
"If one has talent and wisdom,
but his conduct is not good,
is he then acceptable?"
The reply was:
"Why is it so hard for you to understand?
Water can overcome fire,
but can one sheng of water extinguish a forest fire?
Chái was foolish,
but did he ever throw himself into a well?
The gentleman employs benevolence for universal love,
righteousness to eliminate evil,
trustworthiness to establish sincerity,
ritual for self-discipline,
acute hearing for self-examination,
clear vision to observe expressions,
strategy to exercise flexibility,
and wisdom to distinguish things.
How can any of these be lacking?
It is merely a matter of degree.
Moreover, Guǎn Zhòng betrayed his lord and served an enemy;
he was extravagant and violated ritual.
Yet he enabled Duke Huán to achieve the feat of assembling the feudal lords nine times and unifying the world.
Zhòngní praised him, saying:
'Were it not for Guǎn Zhòng,
we would be wearing our hair loose and folding our robes to the left.'
Zhào Hū maintained his integrity and died in hardship,
which is the admirable duty of a minister.
Yet Zhòngní compared him to the petty fidelity of common men and women.
Therefore, the sage values the exceptional ability of talent and wisdom,
which achieves merit and accomplishes deeds that benefit the world.
If faults are many and talent and wisdom are scant,
creating chaos is abundant,
but achieving merit is insufficient,
that is why Zhòngní avoided Yánghuò and executed Shàozhèng Mǎo.
How can such a person be called acceptable?
Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn repeatedly relied on Zhāng Liáng's strategic planning to establish his imperial enterprise.
Although the Four Haos had admirable conduct, what benefit were they in relieving dire distress?
These certainly cannot be discussed on the same day!"
Someone asked:
"Then why did Zhòngní say, 'How can he be called benevolent when he is not wise?'
Does this elevate benevolence?
What does it mean?"
The reply was:
"Benevolence is indeed great,
but Zhòngní said this to make a point,
though it does not mean he belittled wisdom.
If someone were to say:
'That person does not even possess wisdom,
how could he possibly understand benevolence?'
In the past, when King Wǔ died,
King Chéng was young,
and the Duke of Zhōu acted as regent,
Guǎn and Cài incited rebellion in Yīn,
and the Duke of Zhōu executed them.
King Chéng did not understand,
and the Duke of Zhōu feared,
so heaven sent thunder, lightning, wind, and rain to manifest the Duke of Zhōu's virtue,
and only then did King Chéng awaken.
King Chéng was not lacking in benevolence and kindness toward his own flesh and blood,
but merely due to his lack of wisdom and discernment,
he aided the rebels,
nearly destroying the Duke of Zhōu's achievements,
and jeopardizing the legacy of King Wén and King Wǔ.
When Duke Shào saw that the Duke of Zhōu had returned the governance,
yet still did not understand,
and suspected him of coveting power,
the Duke of Zhōu composed the 'Jūn Shì' for him,
and only then was Duke Shào pleased.
Even Duke Shào, with his sagely nature,
was like this!
How much more so for those of lesser pursuits,
who, if they lose a single virtue,
and whose wisdom and strategy are narrow and short,
should indeed be feared!
Zhòngní said:
'One may stand firm with them,
but one cannot adapt with them.'
Mèng Kē said:
'Zǐ Mò held to the mean,
but holding to the mean without adaptability
is like holding to one extreme.'
Zhòngní and Mèng Kē can be said to have understood the essence of adaptable wisdom.
In Yīn, there were three benevolent men:
Wēizǐ, who was as firm as a rock and did not last the day,
Jīzǐ, who faced internal difficulties yet could rectify his will,
and Bǐgān, who remonstrated and had his heart cut out.
The gentleman regards Wēizǐ as the highest,
Jīzǐ as next,
and Bǐgān as the lowest.
Thus, in the Spring and Autumn Annals, when a great officer was killed,
it was always criticized that he could not use wisdom to save himself.
Moreover, King Xú Yǎn knew to cultivate benevolence and righteousness,
but did not know to use force,
and ultimately lost his state.
Duke Yǐn of Lǔ harbored a yielding heart,
but did not recognize flattery and deceit,
and ultimately met his death.
Duke Xiāng of Sòng upheld principles,
but did not know adaptability,
and ultimately was captured.
Bó Zōng of Jìn loved straightforwardness,
but did not understand the changes of the times,
and ultimately perished.
Shūsūn Bào loved goodness,
but did not know how to choose people,
and ultimately met with misfortune and starvation.
These are all examples of treading the path of goodness but lacking wisdom.
Thus, the 'Dàyǎ' values 'being both wise and discerning, to preserve oneself.'
The wise and discerning person
is authoritative but not intimidating,
troubled yet able to find a way through,
resolves doubts and settles uncertainties,
distinguishes things and positions them appropriately.
They avert disaster in its slightest beginnings,
seek blessings before they sprout,
when encountering changing events, they grasp their key,
when dealing with constant matters, they follow their norms;
clever words cannot sway them,
pleasing appearances cannot move them;
their actions are worthy of observation,
and their words serve as a model for teachers.
To compare them to those who merely uphold their will and conduct,
is that not mistaken!"
Someone asked:
"Did the gentlemen of antiquity value rank and emolument?"
The reply was:
"Yes.
The writings of the various masters speak of rank and emolument,
not as something to be valued.
Wealth and resources—not as something to be rich in."
"What does this mean?"
The reply was:
"They encountered times of disorder,
and seeing petty men become wealthy and noble, they spoke thus.
This was not the way of antiquity.
In the ancient system of rank and emolument,
rank was to reside with the virtuous,
emolument was to nourish the meritorious.
Those with great merit had ample emolument,
those with far-reaching virtue had lofty rank;
those with small merit had meager emolument,
those with limited virtue had humble rank.
Therefore, by observing their rank,
one could distinguish their virtue.
By seeing their emolument,
one could know their merit.
There was no need to ask.
The gentlemen of antiquity valued rank and emolument
for this reason.
Not for the splendor of embroidered robes upon their persons,
nor for the satisfaction of fine meats in their mouths.
Not for the delight of beautiful colors before their eyes,
nor for the pleasure of bells and drums in their ears.
Confucius said:
'When the state is well-governed,
to be poor and lowly
is a disgrace.'
When an enlightened king reigns above,
ordering ranks and distributing emoluments, yet one is not included,
the gentleman considers it the utmost shame—
how could there be any lowliness in it?
When the former kings were about to establish the feudal lords and bestow ranks and emoluments,
they would surely do so in the pure temple,
displaying the music of metal and stone,
holding feasts and bestowing gifts,
with the temple officers assisting,
and the court scribe composing the record.
The 'Ode' says:
'King Wén has toiled diligently,
and I receive it.
Spread this and think upon it:
I go forth seeking stability,
this is the mandate of Zhōu.
Oh, think upon it!'
From this we see that
rank and emolument were valued by the former kings,
not taken lightly.
Thus, the 'Shū' says:
'Do not leave offices vacant,
for the work of heaven
is to be carried out by men.'"
"The lowliness of noble ranks and emoluments
stems from those who occupy them being unworthy;
to despise the person
is to despise the position.
Their nobility
stems from those who occupy them being worthy;
to honor the person
is to honor the position.
The Book of Songs says:
'The noble lord arrives,
in embroidered robes and patterned gowns.
His jade pendants clink and clang,
may he live long and never be forgotten.'
Embroidered robes and patterned gowns are what the noble lord wears;
because his virtue is cherished,
his attire is thus admired.
A tyrannical and chaotic ruler is not without such attire,
yet the people do not admire it.
Position is likewise.
In the past, the Duke of Zhōu assisted the royal house in ruling the world,
his sagely virtue was illustrious and renowned,
his royal achievements were vast and great.
King Chéng enfeoffed him with the territory of Shàohào,
a land seven hundred lǐ square,
bestowing upon him mountains, rivers, fields, and soil,
with vassals and all necessary provisions,
official registers and administrative offices,
ritual vessels, dragon banners with nine tassels,
to sacrifice to the Di in the suburbs.
Tàigōng assisted King Wǔ in conquering Shāng and pacifying chaos,
the king enfeoffed him with the territory of Shuǎngjiūshì,
extending east to the sea,
west to the Hé River,
south to Mùlíng,
north to Wúdì.
'The five marquises and nine earls,
you shall indeed subdue them,'
and for generations, he served as Grand Tutor, pacifying and governing the eastern Xià.
At that time,
who would say that wealth and nobility were not glorious and favored?
From that time onward,
the teachings of Wén and Wǔ declined,
the principles of promotion and demotion were abandoned;
the feudal lords usurped power and acted wantonly,
the great officers held hereditary positions;
people were ennobled not for their virtue,
people were granted emoluments not for their merit;
there were those who stole the state and became noble,
those who stole land and became rich;
the treacherous and wicked achieved their desires,
the benevolent and worthy lost their aspirations.
Thus, wealth and nobility came to be reviled and criticized.
Therefore, Confucius said:
'When a state is without the Way,
to be wealthy and noble
is a disgrace.'
Thus, whether wealth and nobility are good or evil depends on the age.
The Book of Changes says:
'The great treasure of the sage is called position.'
Why is it said that the great treasure of the sage is 'position'?
Position is the loom for establishing virtue,
power is the shuttle for practicing righteousness.
The sage treads the loom and grasps the shuttle,
weaving the transformations of heaven and earth,
causing all things to follow in harmony,
and human relations to be rectified.
Within the six directions,
each fulfills their desires;
is it not fitting that this is called the great treasure?
Therefore, the sage considers the lack of power and position as destitution,
the hundred craftsmen consider the lack of tools as hardship;
hardship means the loss of resources,
destitution means the abandonment of the Way.
Thus, Confucius wandered restlessly without settling,
precisely because he worried about the abandonment of the Way.
The Book of Changes says:
'The well is cleansed, yet none drink from it;
this saddens my heart.
It can be drawn from;
if the king is enlightened,
all will receive its blessings.'
"To ascend a height and raise a banner,
then what one sees is broad;
to follow the wind and shake a bell,
then what one hears reaches far.
It is not that the banner's colors become brighter,
nor that the bell's sound becomes louder;
it is because of what they rely upon that this is so.
How much more so for one who occupies a position of wealth and nobility,
and implements his governance and decrees.
Thus, when Shùn was a commoner, he was still an ordinary man,
but when he received the mandate at Wéngǔ,
and was called 'the One Man,'
then the Queen Mother of the West came to present a white jade ring.
When the Duke of Zhōu was a feudal lord, he was still a minister,
but when he ascended the throne at the Bright Hall,
standing with his back to the axe-screen,
then the Yuècháng clan came to present a white pheasant.
Therefore, if one's person is not honored, one's influence will not shine;
if one's position is not high, one's transformation will not be broad.
The Book of Changes says:
'The Fēng hexagram signifies success,
there is no blame.
The king attains it.
Do not worry,
it is fitting at midday.'
This refers to the person being honored and the position being high.
This matter
is what the sage strives for.
Nevertheless,
seeking it requires the Way,
obtaining it depends on fate.
Shùn, Yǔ, and Confucius can be said to have sought it with the Way.
Shùn and Yǔ obtained it,
Confucius did not obtain it;
this can be said to be due to fate.
Not only sages,
but also worthies are like this.
Jì, Xiè, Bóyì, Yīyǐn, and Fùyuè are those who obtained it;
Yányuān, Mǐnzǐqiān, Rǎngēng, and Zhònggōng are those who did not obtain it.
Therefore, a good farmer does not worry about the fields not being cultivated,
but worries about the wind and rain not being timely;
a noble man does not worry about virtue and morality not being established,
but worries about not encountering the right time and age.
The Book of Songs says:
'I drive those four stallions,
the four stallions with stout necks.
I gaze at the four directions,
cramped and with nowhere to gallop.'
This laments the Way not being encountered.
Is it only for one age?
Is it only for one age?"
Since Confucius passed away,
it has been several hundred years to this day.
During this time, no sage has arisen,
the laws of Táng and Yú have declined,
the teachings of the Three Dynasties have ceased.
The Great Way has deteriorated,
the principles of human relations are unstable,
thus those who confuse the age and steal fame,
taking advantage of the people having long been separated from the sagely teachings,
give rise to heretical doctrines,
create aberrant techniques,
using the legacy of the ancient kings as a pretext to embellish them,
identical in form but contrary in substance,
similar in appearance but distant in spirit,
claiming to have attained the true essence of the sage,
each with their own theories and special arguments, deceiving the people of an entire age,
enticing them with falsely achieved fame,
frightening them with baseless slanders,
causing people to waver between gain and loss,
anxious and unsettled,
losing their original nature,
unaware of their own delusion,
all following and promoting their practices, indulging and favoring them.
These techniques among the people
are like internal blockages of disease,
not causing pain, itching, or discomfort in the body,
the mind and will remain clear and unaware,
yet the illness has already deepened.
However, when the appointed day arrives,
the vital energy suddenly exhausts.
Therefore, internal blockages of disease
are illnesses that cause premature death,
and what Biǎnquè greatly detested,
because even Lúyī could not distinguish them,
and those afflicted could not counteract them.
In the past, Yáng Zhū, Mò Dí, Shēn Bùhài, Hán Fēi, Tián Pián, and Gōngsūn Lóng muddled and disordered the Way of the former kings,
running rampant in the age of the Warring States,
yet they were not the great calamity of human relations.
Why?
Their techniques, being different from those of the sages, were easy to distinguish,
and those who followed them were few.
Now, those who seek fame differ from the sages only subtly;
looking at them, it is difficult to perceive,
and the world does not condemn them;
listening to them, it is difficult to hear,
and the world does not expose them.
Why is this?
They toil in distant pursuits to glorify themselves,
cloaking it as a dislike for stubbornness;
they seek broadly to win over the multitude,
cloaking it as benevolence and love;
they twist the straight to gain recommendation,
cloaking it as adapting to the times;
they bend the Way to silence criticism,
cloaking it as fear and love;
they know much about the ways of the vulgar,
crudely recite the texts of the *Book of Songs* and the *Book of Documents*,
cloaking it as broad learning;
they adorn their faults and speak pleasingly,
lack proper principles yet their words seem discerning,
cloaking it as understanding reason;
they reside only among talented people,
travel only to the imperial capital,
cloaking it as observing customs;
yet they delight in changing their names,
making themselves hard to find,
cloaking it as being able to be tranquil;
they humble and bend their bodies,
soften and gentle their countenances,
cloaking it as warmth and respect;
yet at times they reject and cut off,
striking decisively and severely,
cloaking it as independence;
they encourage and nurture the young and ignorant,
instructing them with their own methods,
cloaking it as diligent teaching;
they treat themselves like gold and jade,
to make their words seem divine,
cloaking it as expounding the Way;
this is their general manner.
If they can gain fame,
even without necessarily achieving substance,
they do not refrain;
if they can achieve substance,
even without necessarily gaining fame,
they do not rest.
Anxiously, they constantly fear not being respected in their own time;
hurriedly, they also fear not being esteemed by later generations.
Their hearts are troubled within,
their forms toiled without,
yet their clever adjustments are sufficient to manage it,
their skillful dexterity sufficient to dignify it,
their analogies and comparisons sufficient to fill it out,
their literary phrases and vocal tones sufficient to adorn it.
Therefore, desire appears like modesty,
agitation appears like calm,
obscurity appears like clarity,
lameness appears like uprightness.
Examining their origins,
they are not from the laws of Yáo and Shùn;
investigating their source,
they are not from the school of Zhòngní.
They are deviant and unmeasured,
dried up and without a source,
incapable of guiding by principle to reach far,
discerning things to accomplish transformation.
These are the masters of the cunning;
the outstanding among the false.
Yet those of middling talent,
all bow and praise them,
raise their voices to echo them;
after their death, they discuss their lasting deeds,
harmed by them yet still regretting they could not match them.
Alas!
How deeply are people submerged and drowned!
Confucius said:
"Do not worry that others do not know you."
Even if someone tells me, "I do good,"
I do not believe it.
Why?
Because the spring does not well up from within,
but the water poured in comes from outside.
If it is like this,
then the mind that abides in the Way is not clear,
and the intention that holds to righteousness is not evident.
Even if they rely on the former kings and cite the *Book of Songs* and *Book of Documents*,
what benefit will it be?
With this, they poison the people of the world,
causing all to turn from the root toward the branch,
affairs to be accomplished through falseness,
in chaotic disorder,
rushing about without cease.
Their influence in the world
reaches the point where fathers steal their sons' reputations,
elder brothers pilfer their younger brothers' praise,
flesh and blood deceive each other,
friends defraud one another.
This is the path to great chaos.
Therefore, the pursuit of fame
is what the sages most strictly forbid.
In the past, Duke Mèng of Wèi often acted without propriety,
incurring the hatred of the people of the state.
Qí Bào killed him to make a name for himself.
The *Spring and Autumn Annals* records him as "a robber."
Its commentary says:
"Therefore, the noble man, when acting, thinks of propriety;
when conducting himself, thinks of righteousness.
He does not turn back for profit,
nor feel remorse over unrighteousness.
Some seek fame and do not attain it;
some wish to cover up, yet their fame becomes clear.
This punishes unrighteousness.
