Qí Bào was Minister of Crime of Wèi,
a hereditary high officer.
He acted unrighteously,
so he is recorded as 'a robber.'
Zhū Shùqí of Zhū, Móu Yí of Jǔ, and Hēi Gōng of Zhū left with their lands,
seeking sustenance only,
not seeking fame.
Though lowly, they are necessarily recorded.
These two cases serve to punish recklessness and remove greed.
If one endangers his own person,
puts the great men in peril and danger,
and yet his fame becomes clear and widespread,
then those who attack difficulties will rush to it.
If one steals a city and betrays his lord to seek great profit without gaining fame,
then greedy and reckless people will exert their strength for it.
Therefore, the *Spring and Autumn Annals* records Qí Bào as 'a robber,'
and names the three traitors,
to punish unrighteousness,
to enumerate evil and lack of propriety.
This is its good purpose."
The questioner says:
"Qí Bào killed a man to make a name for himself,
so Zhòngní detested him and called him 'a robber.'
Do those who seek fame today have the crime of killing?"
The reply:
"In the *Spring and Autumn Annals*,
those who kill are not few,
yet they are not all called 'robbers.'
The sages' judgment of good and evil
must weigh the gravity,
consider the numbers to determine it.
Those who seek fame cause truth and falsehood to obscure each other,
right and wrong to exchange places,
and the people to be misled.
This is a great disaster for the state and family.
Killing a man is the harm of one person.
How can they be compared?
Then why select the killer to record as 'robber'?
Xún Qīng also said:
'Stealing a name is worse than stealing goods.'
The village honest man also has no crime of killing,
yet Zhòngní detested him.
Why?
Because he confounds virtue.
Now, those with false names who confound virtue,
are they only what is meant by the village honest man?
All affairs are mixed and tangled,
changing circumstances multiply,
the ways of confounding virtue
are certainly not limited to one aspect.
The *Book of Documents* says:
'Quiet words but contrary deeds,
outwardly respectful but flooding Heaven with pride.'
All are categories of confounding virtue.
The *Outer Commentary to the Spring and Autumn Annals* says:
'Counterfeiting benevolence is frivolity;
counterfeiting propriety is shame;
counterfeiting courage is villainy.'
Benevolence, propriety, and courage
are the beauties of the Way.
Yet if one practices them not with correctness,
then one cannot avoid great evil.
Therefore, the noble man, regarding the Way,
examines how he holds to it,
is cautious in how he practices it."
The questioner asked:
"Confucius disliked dying without having one's name recognized,
and also detested false reputation.
So what should one adhere to?"
The reply was:
"Why should this be considered strange?
Names are what designate reality,
reality is established and names follow it,
it is not that names are established and reality follows them.
Thus, when a long form is established, it is named 'long',
when a short form is established, it is named 'short'.
It is not that the names 'long' and 'short' are established first,
and then the forms of long and short follow them.
What Confucius valued
was the name that corresponds to reality.
Valuing the name is precisely how one values reality.
The connection of names to reality
is like things being tied to their seasons.
Things: in spring,
they sprout blossoms; in summer,
they spread leaves; in autumn,
they wither and fall; in winter,
they bear fruit—this happens naturally without deliberate action.
If forced,
their nature is harmed.
Names are the same,
so false names are all intended to harm it.
People only know that having a good name is virtuous,
but do not realize that false virtue is not virtuous.
How deluded they are!
There are three ways of seeking fame:
seeking much from little,
seeking speed from slowness,
seeking something from nothing.
These three, unless one resorts to dark and obscure means,
deviating from the right path,
cannot be achieved.
Certainly, these are not what a gentleman can do.
A gentleman is one who can perfect his heart,
when the heart is perfected, the inner self is settled,
when the inner self is settled, external things cannot disturb it,
when external things cannot disturb it, he finds joy alone in his Way,
finding joy alone in his Way, what is unheard becomes heard,
what is unmanifest becomes manifest.
Thus, the *Book of Rites* says: 'The Way of the gentleman,
though obscure, becomes increasingly evident day by day;
the way of the petty person,
though glaring, perishes day by day.
The Way of the gentleman,
is plain yet not tiresome,
simple yet elegant,
gentle yet principled,
knowing the near in the distant,
knowing the source of the wind,
knowing the manifest in the subtle,
thus one can enter into virtue.'
"What makes the gentleman unreachable,
is precisely what others do not see."
Being thus,
how could he be restless in a chaotic world,
seeking to transform the unacknowledged mediocrity of ordinary people?"
Do people's fondness for socializing
not compare to the age of sage kings?
In ancient times, not socializing
was for self-cultivation, was it not?
In the past, when sage kings governed their people,
they assigned them the nine duties,
disciplined them with the eight punishments,
guided them with the five rites,
instructed them with the six types of music,
taught them with the three principles,
and trained them with the six forms of conduct,
so that the people labored without reaching exhaustion,
and rested without falling into idleness.
At that time,
within the four seas,
people advanced in virtue and cultivated their work,
diligently attending to affairs without leisure,
how would they dare indulge their hearts, abandon their efforts, engage in unnecessary activities, and harm their rest and achievements?
From kings and dukes down to the various officers,
none failed to be upright and reverent,
each respectfully fulfilling their duties,
not daring to indulge in leisure or idleness.
Thus, the *Guoyu* says:
"At dawn, the Son of Heaven, in grand attire, pays homage to the sun,
and with the Three Dukes and Nine Ministers, acknowledges the virtues of the earth;
at midday, he examines governance,
and with the various officials' administrative affairs,
the ministers, commanders, and local governors orderly carry out civil matters;
at dusk, in lesser attire, he pays homage to the moon,
and with the Grand Historian and the Director of Astrology, reverently observes the celestial laws;
after sunset, he supervises the nine palace officials,
ensuring they purify and present the offerings for the Di and suburban sacrifices,
and only then does he rest.
The feudal lords, in the morning, attend to the Son of Heaven's decrees and tasks,
during the day, examine their state duties,
in the evening, review their laws and punishments,
at night, alert their various artisans,
ensuring they do not become negligent or indulgent,
and only then do they rest.
The high ministers and grand officers, in the morning, examine their duties,
during the day, discuss their various administrative affairs,
in the evening, arrange their tasks,
at night, manage their household matters,
and only then do they rest.
The officers, in the morning, receive their tasks,
during the day, study and practice them,
in the evening, review and repeat them,
at night, reflect on their faults without regret,
and only then do they rest."
At the beginning of the year, the officials are ordered by the government:
"Each of you, attend to your duties,
examine your laws,
prepare your affairs,
to await the king's commands.
If any are disrespectful,
the state will impose severe punishment."
From this perspective,
not engaging in socializing
is not a flaw in governance,
but because the mind is focused on duties and there is no leisure for it.
Moreover, in the teachings of the former kings,
officials did not guide the people toward socializing,
and in local assessments of virtue,
socializing was not used to recommend the worthy,
thus, without prohibiting the people,
the people naturally abandoned it.
By the decline of the Zhōu dynasty,
socializing became prevalent.
The questioner asked:
"You, in your writings,
claim that gentlemen engage in socializing
to seek worthy friends;
now you say socializing is not ancient,
so did ancient gentlemen have no worthy friends?"
The reply was:
"How strange!
You do not understand the great principles.
If one does not leave the courtyard,
sitting in an empty room,
even ghosts and spirits
will not see me,
let alone worthy people.
Now, you do not examine the reality of what I call socializing,
but quibble over the name.
There are names that are the same but realities that differ.
There are names that differ but realities that are the same.
Thus, regarding this matter, the gentleman
focuses on the reality
and does not criticize the name.
When I speak of ancient people not socializing,
I do not mean they stayed hidden in dark rooms;
when I speak of modern people fond of socializing,
I do not mean they are always drenched by rain on the road.
Ancient gentlemen, during intervals in royal affairs,
would present gifts to meet their colleagues
and the worthy within the state.
In their feasts and pleasures,
they spoke of benevolence and righteousness, not fame and profit.
Gentlemen without official appointments
also, during breaks in agricultural work,
presented gifts to meet their local comrades
and the worthy of ancient times.
So why would they not gain worthy friends?
They did not abandon royal duties, neglect their work, travel to distant lands, or waste years.
Thus, ancient socializing was close,
modern socializing is distant;
ancient socializing was few,
modern socializing is many;
ancient socializing was for seeking the worthy,
modern socializing is only for fame and profit."
"In ancient times, when establishing a state, there were four categories of people:
those who held contracts, maintained maps and records,
upheld the laws of the sage kings,
and governed with the principles of ritual and righteousness,
were called shì;
those who exerted their strength to maximize the benefits of the land,
were called farmers;
those who examined the straight and curved, shapes and forms,
prepared the five materials to distinguish the tools of the people,
were called the hundred artisans;
those who circulated the rare treasures from all directions to supply them,
were called merchants and travelers.
Each generation continued their respective tasks,
never changing their occupations.
From youth, they practiced them,
their hearts settled into them,
and it became as if by nature, so their efforts never ceased.
Therefore, in their dwelling,
each followed their own clan,
not allowing interference,
so as to unify their eyes and ears.
Those who did not diligently pursue these four occupations
were called destitute people,
and were conscripted into penal labor.
In all matters of the people's comings and goings, movements and stops,
gatherings and meals,
there were regulations,
and they were not permitted to be idle or neglectful,
so as not to hinder the affairs of livelihood,
and thus incur crimes and punishments.
How then could there be those who roamed beyond the norms,
and devoted themselves solely to socializing?
Therefore, five households formed a bǐ,
making them mutually responsible.
The bǐ had a leader.
Five bǐ formed a lǘ,
making them mutually supportive,
and the lǘ had a xū.
Four lǘ formed a zú,
making them assist in burials,
and the zú had a shī.
Five zú formed a dǎng,
making them rescue each other,
and the dǎng had a zhèng.
Five dǎng formed a zhōu,
making them provide relief,
and the zhōu had a zhǎng.
Five zhōu formed a xiāng,
making them treat each other as guests,
and the xiāng had a dàfū.
There must be intelligent, compassionate, and benevolent individuals
to each oversee the governance, education, decrees, and prohibitions of their xiāng.
On the auspicious day of the first month,
they received the laws from the Sītú,
then returned and promulgated them to their zhōu, dǎng, zú, and lǘ,
and to the various officials of the bǐ,
having each instruct the people under their governance,
to examine their moral conduct,
observe their skills and arts,
and report them annually.
The dàfū observed their numbers,
and whenever among the people there were those with moral conduct and skills,
the bǐ reported to the lǘ,
the lǘ reported to the zú,
the zú reported to the dǎng,
the dǎng reported to the zhōu,
the zhōu reported to the xiāng,
and the xiāng reported upward.
If among the people there were those guilty of strange and wicked deeds,
the bǐ reported it,
following the same procedure.
If there was goodness and it was not reported,
it was called concealing the worthy,
and concealing the worthy was punishable;
if there was evil and it was not reported,
it was called colluding with rebels,
and colluding with rebels was also punishable.
Therefore, the people could not leave goodness unreported,
nor could they conceal evil.
Every three years, the xiāng dàfū conducted a grand review and promoted the worthy and capable.
The xiāng elders, along with the xiāng dàfū and various officials, presented the records of the worthy and capable to the king,
who bowed and received them,
and stored them in the heavenly archives.
When appointing them to ranks,
each was assigned according to their suitability,
not placing the great in charge of the small,
nor burdening the light with heavy responsibilities.
Therefore, the Shū says:
'All officials emulate each other,
all artisans are timely.'
This was the method by which the ancient kings selected shì and appointed officials.
Thus, the people all returned to their roots and sought within themselves,
were cautious of virtue and accumulated small deeds,
knowing that blessings and fortune did not come from others;
therefore, there were no affairs of socializing,
no beginnings of requests and entrustments;
their minds were clear, their bodies tranquil,
serene and self-content;
all led each other along the correct path,
encouraged each other with sincerity and honesty,
deceitful talk did not arise,
and wickedness naturally ceased.
"In the decline of the age,
above there were no enlightened Son of Heaven,
below there were no worthy feudal lords;
rulers did not distinguish right from wrong,
ministers did not discern black from white;
selecting shì did not proceed from the xiāng and dǎng,
examining conduct did not base itself on family merits;
those with many supporters were considered talented and worthy,
those with few supporters were deemed unworthy;
ranking nobility listened to unsubstantiated discussions,
distributing emoluments adopted the rumors of the regions.
When the people saw it was like this,
they knew that wealth and honor could be achieved by following the crowd,
that fame and reputation could be obtained through empty clamor,
so they left their fathers and elder brothers,
departed from their villages and neighborhoods,
did not cultivate skills and arts,
did not govern their moral conduct,
discussed theories that suited the times,
formed cliques and factions,
anxious and hurried,
with not a day to settle,
praising and extolling each other in turn,
acting as each other's front and back.
Chaos was born,
splendor withered.
Commoners who deceived the ruler,
deluded the prime minister,
stole elections,
and usurped honors and favors
were too numerous to count.
Those who had already gained success considered themselves worthy and pressed on,
while the envious raced to catch up,
and everywhere it was the same.
Who could avoid being like this?
The reigns of Emperor Huán and Emperor Líng were especially severe.
From the highest ministers and dàfū down to regional governors and commandery administrators,
they did not attend to royal affairs,
but made receiving guests their priority.
Carriages and caps filled their gates,
scholars' robes blocked the roads.
They had no time to eat when hungry,
no rest when weary.
Bustling and swarming,
they turned night into day.
Down to the minor officials,
the magistrates of cities with black silk cords,
none failed to consult each other on gaining followers,
boasting of humbling themselves to receive shì.
They traveled by starlight at dawn,
sending off and welcoming guests,
relay stations constantly full,
clerks and soldiers transmitting inquiries,
torches lighting night journeys,
gatekeepers never closing the gates,
clasping arms and gripping wrists,
pointing to heaven and swearing oaths.
They claimed deep friendships,
without weighing importance,
official documents piled up in government offices,
prisoners accumulated in jails,
yet they had no time to attend to them.
Examining their actions in detail,
it was not out of concern for the state or compassion for the people, nor for discussing the Way and virtue,
but merely for managing their own affairs, seeking power, and chasing profit.
There were those whose names were registered at court,
yet called themselves disciples of wealthy and noble households—
such cases filled every house.
Acting as teachers without teaching anything,
and disciples not receiving instruction,
yet in their affairs,
they even bore the appearance of men,
but adopted the demeanor of maidservants and concubines.
Some offered goods and bribes
to secure themselves,
seeking recommendations and entrustments,
scheming for official advancement.
Yet they cast glances and pointed with palms,
spoke loudly and boastfully.
Such types as these—
speaking of it is still shameful,
yet those who do it feel no disgrace.
Alas!
The corruption of royal teachings
has reached such a state!"
Someone asked:
"Confucius said, 'The benevolent live long,'
yet Yán Yuān died young;
'Families that accumulate goodness will have abundant blessings,'
yet Bǐ Gān and Zǐ Xū met with great calamities.
Could it be that the sage's words are untrustworthy and deceive later generations?"
Therefore, the Minister of Works, Xún Shuàng of Yǐngchuān, discussed this,
believing that the ancients had a saying:
"To die but not perish,"
meaning "The highest is to establish virtue,
the next is to establish achievements,
and the next is to establish words."
Though the body perishes,
the way remains.
Thus it is called "immortality."
Now, the physical form is the essence and spirit of a person,
while virtue, righteousness, and a good reputation are the glory and splendor of that essence and spirit.
The noble person cherishes their physical form,
and thus cultivates their virtue and righteousness.
The physical form is inherently something that decays and perishes;
whether one lives long or not,
it is only a matter of several decades.
But whether virtue and righteousness are established or not
differs by thousands of years—
how can they be spoken of in the same breath!
In Yán Yuān's time, there were people who lived a hundred years,
but who now still knows their names?
The Book of Songs says:
"For ten thousand years and a thousand,
may your eyebrows be long and free from harm."
How can people live for ten thousand or a thousand years?
This refers to enduring virtue.
From this perspective,
'The benevolent live long'—how can it be untrustworthy!
The Commentary says:
"There are things one loves more than life,
and things one hates more than death."
Bǐ Gān and Zǐ Xū were both people who valued righteousness over life;
by sacrificing what they held lightly,
they gained what they valued greatly.
Seeking benevolence, they attained benevolence—
this can indeed be called a blessing!"
"Striking bells and chimes
is to produce their sound;
boiling sacrificial wine and burning incense
is to spread their fragrance.
The hardship, persecution, and humiliation of the worthy
are like the striking of the bell;
their death, drowning, or peril
are like the boiling and burning.
Sūn Áo of Běihǎi believed that life and death are determined by fate,
not caused by others.
If accumulating goodness brings blessings,
and practicing benevolence leads to longevity,
this is the meaning of moral instruction—
to guide people toward goodness.
If it were said:
'Accumulating goodness brings no reward,
and practicing benevolence leads to misfortune,'
then foolish and confused people
would turn to evil and defy the natural order.
Therefore it is said:
'The people can be made to follow,
but cannot be made to understand.'
'Our bodies, hair, and skin
are received from our parents;
we dare not injure or harm them.
This is the height of filial piety.'
As for those who seek fame,
mutilating their bodies,
braving danger and persecution,
to sacrifice themselves for fame—
even Zēng Shēn would not do such a thing.
Zǐ Xū defied his ruler and went to an enemy state,
to wash away his shame
and avenge his father.
He violated the rites of a minister,
encouraged the roots of rebellion and regicide,
and failed to deeply understand the different capacities of the two rulers.
In the end, his head was displayed without decaying—
this is the greatest of misfortunes;
what blessing is there in this?"
Gàn believed that both arguments missed the true principle.
Thus he wrote "Discourse on Longevity and Premature Death," saying:
"I have heard the ancients said that what is detested in the wise is forcing interpretations—
is this not so?
Therefore, when a noble person formulates an argument,
they must trace the appropriate categories of things and follow principle.
Thus it is said:
'When the explanation is complete, it cannot be refuted;
when the meaning is established, it cannot be confused.'
If there were no such difficulties,
one might violate the root and die,
and still not grasp the reality.
The words of the sage are broad!
And great!
Their transformations and actions
cannot be uniformly measured.
Now I will recklessly list the categories to clarify their errors.
Longevity is of three kinds:
there is longevity from royal beneficence,
longevity of reputation,
and longevity from practicing benevolence.
The Book of Documents says:
'The five blessings:
the first is "longevity."'
This is longevity from royal beneficence.
The Book of Songs says:
'His virtue is without fault,
and his long life is not forgotten.'
This is longevity of reputation.
Confucius said:
'The benevolent live long.'
This is longevity from practicing benevolence.
Confucius said:
'Thus, the benevolent live long.'
Benevolence benefits all things,
and all things receive its benefit.
Therefore, they must live long.
"If Xún considered 'dying but not perishing' as longevity,
then why does the Book of Documents say:
'In the past, King Zhōngzōng of Yīn,
reverently respectful and awed by the Mandate of Heaven, measured himself,
governed the people with reverence and caution,
daring not to indulge in idleness or ease.
Thus, Zhōngzōng enjoyed the throne for seventy-five years.
As for Gāozōng,
he toiled long abroad,
living among the common people.
When he ascended the throne,
he observed the mourning hut,
and did not speak for three years.
Because he did not speak,
when he did speak, it was harmonious.
He dared not indulge in idleness or ease,
bringing peace and prosperity to the Yīn state.
From great to small,
none had cause for complaint.
Thus, Gāozōng enjoyed the throne for fifty-nine years.
As for Zǔ Jiǎ,
he considered it unrighteous to be king,
and long lived as a commoner.
When he ascended the throne,
he understood the concerns of the common people,
was able to protect and benefit the masses,
and did not oppress the widowed or orphaned.
Thus, Zǔ Jiǎ enjoyed the throne for thirty-three years.
From that time onward, the kings who were established
were born to leisure!
They did not know the hardships of farming,
nor the toil and suffering of the common people.
They only pursued indulgence and pleasure.
From that time onward,
none were able to enjoy long life—
some ten years,
some seven or eight years,
some five or six years,
some three or four years.'
Could the Duke of Zhōu not understand the meaning of longevity and premature death?
Thus, speaking of longevity of reputation
cannot be equated with reputation alone.
Therefore, the enlightened person must consider all aspects.
"Sūn focused solely on the meaning of royal instruction,
fearing that foolish and confused people would defy the natural order.
Why then did Confucius say:
'There are those who kill themselves to accomplish benevolence,
but none who seek life at the expense of benevolence.'
And also:
'Since ancient times, all must die,
but without trust, the people cannot stand.'
He wanted them to know that abandoning food means certain death.
Did Confucius then want the people to be without benevolence and trust?
The teachings of the sage
are for the clear and sincere noble person—
how could they be merely for the foolish and confused people?
Foolish and confused people are restrained by the punishment of axe and halberd,
deterred by the penalties of branding and tattooing,
relocated to other cities,
and exiled to distant lands.
Even then, some do not reform—
how much less through words alone?
Thus it is said:
'Only the highest wisdom and the lowest stupidity do not change.'
Thus, the arguments of Xún and Sūn
both miss the true reality,
and this can be understood."
"In ancient times, before Emperor Kù, it is too remote to discuss.
As for the affairs of the Táng, Yú, and the Three Dynasties, can they be briefly understood?
I have heard that from Yáo to King Wǔ,
from Jì to Zhōu and Shào,
all were benevolent men.
The number of rulers and ministers was not small,
and examining their lifespans, they were not short-lived.
Is this not evidence that 'the benevolent enjoy longevity'?
Moreover, were the seventy disciples of Confucius cruel people?
It is merely that their benevolence varied in quality.
Among them, only Yán Huí died young.
To base doubts about the rest on Yán Huí alone
is no different from weighing a hook of gold
against a cartload of feathers,
and saying:
'Gold is lighter than feathers.'
The Way of Heaven is vast and distant,
obscure and difficult to comprehend.
The sages took the general principles to establish enduring models;
how could they possibly attend to every detail without error,
leaving not the slightest discrepancy?
Furthermore, nothing is more reliable than the four seasons,
yet sometimes spring does not bring blossoms,
summer may see frost fall,
autumn may bring rain and snow,
and winter may lack ice.
How can we then consider it difficult?
So-called misfortune is when one wishes to avoid it but instead encounters it.
Bǐ Gān and Wǔ Zǐxū knew the inevitable outcome yet willingly pursued it!
What fault lies with Heaven?
Even if Heaven wishes to bless the benevolent,
it cannot reach out with arms to save them from death.
This does not mean there is no reward.
If Xún were to raise this objection
and explain it by beating and burning,
it would be of no practical use.
Mr. Sūn's criticism of Bǐ Gān and Wǔ Zǐxū
is also unreasonable.
The Yīn dynasty had three benevolent men,
and Bǐ Gān was one of them.
Why must one die with hands open to be considered virtuous?
Although Wǔ Zǐxū had the fault of enmity toward his ruler,
his heart can still be seen as benevolent.
His head displayed without decay
indeed reflects a minister's integrity.
Moreover, the Way of the worthy
leads to the same end by different paths,
achieves the same goal through diverse thoughts.
Some see danger and give their lives,
some see goodness and withdraw far away,
some let their hair down and sing wildly,
some are dismissed three times yet do not leave,
some decline offers and dwell in mountains,
some endure humiliation and stoop to serve.
How can they all be judged by the standards of a sage?
Alas!
Those who understand integrity
truly grasp this matter.
They examine it carefully, that is all."
The greatest flaw in a ruler
lies in being meticulous about minor matters
while neglecting the great Way;
scrutinizing what is near
while being blind to long-term plans.
Therefore, from ancient times to the present,
there has never been such a case without disorder,
nor such a case without ruin.
Being meticulous about minor matters
and scrutinizing what is near
means the ears delight in the harmony of music and songs,
the eyes gaze upon the patterns of carvings and colors,
the mouth is quick with clever and sharp retorts,
the mind comprehends short tales and trivial writings,
the hands practice the skills of archery, charioteering, calligraphy, and arithmetic,
the body strives in the postures of bowing, turning, and bending.
All these things,
observing them can fully occupy a person's mind,
learning them can easily stir a person's ambitions.
Moreover, these are the lesser teachings of the former kings;
without some small talent and wit,
one could not even accomplish them.
Therefore, those who can do them
all take pleasure in their pursuits,
and do not seek approval from others,
because others are generally incapable.
Now, a ruler who holds the dignity of facing south,
wielding the power of life and death,
his position is already sufficient to surpass others.
If he adds to this the ability to surpass others,
harboring a self-righteous heart,
who would dare oppose him?
Even if a common man acts this way,
none dare admonish him,
let alone a ruler?
Thus, his crimes pile up like mountains, yet he does not see them;
criticisms roar like thunder, yet he does not hear them.
Is this not extreme?
Minor matters are sweet to the taste,
while the great Way is pure and bland.
What is near is easy to verify,
while long-term plans are difficult to prove effective.
Only a greatly enlightened gentleman can master both.
Therefore, most are deluded by sweetness,
unable to reach the bland;
dazzled by the easy,
unable to return to the difficult.
Hence, well-governed reigns are few,
while chaotic reigns are many.
Therefore, what a ruler must devote himself to
lies in the great Way and long-term plans!
The great Way and long-term plans mean:
being benevolent enough to nurture all living beings,
kind enough to care for the common people,
perceptive enough to illuminate the four directions,
wise enough to govern all things,
authoritative enough to respond to endless changes,
righteous enough to enrich resources and wealth,
威严 enough to suppress wickedness and wrongdoing,
martial enough to quell disasters and chaos,
careful in listening and receiving counsel,
and discerning in appointing officials.
Understanding the origins of rise and fall,
comprehending the distinction between safety and danger—
if so, then the Way of rulership is complete.
It is not that rulers lack the ability to govern,
but that they lose sight of priorities.
The Way has fundamentals and peripherals,
affairs have lightness and weight.
What distinguishes sages from ordinary people
is nothing else
but this alone.
Duke Huán of Lǔ was handsome in appearance
and skilled in many arts,
yet he lacked the great talent and wisdom of a ruler.
He could not use ritual to restrain and correct his mother,
allowing her to engage in incessant debauchery with the Marquis of Qí,
galloping about on the roads.
Therefore, the *Shī* satirizes him, saying:
'Ah, how famous!
Beautiful eyes so clear.
The ceremony is complete,
all day shooting at the target,
never missing the center.
Truly our nephew!'
Later, Duke Zhāo
was also adept in the practice of graceful demeanor,
which he frequently displayed when attending the court of Jìn.
From the greeting at the outskirts to the presentation of gifts,
he never violated ritual.
However, he did not attend to state affairs;
governance lay with the great officers,
and he could not reclaim it.
Zǐjiā Jī was worthy,
but he could not employ him.
He violated the clear prohibitions of a great state,
oppressed and abused smaller states,
profited from others' difficulties,
yet did not recognize his own peril.
The ducal house split into four,
and the people fed off others.
Their thoughts were not with the duke,
and he did not plan for the end.
Finally, he suffered the calamity of fleeing into exile.
The *Chūnqiū* records and condemns him, saying:
'The duke fled to Qí,
and halted at Yángzhōu.'
Therefore, the *Chūnqiū Wàizhuàn* says:
'For a ruler of a state, it is beautiful to be clothed in favor,
joyful to bring peace to the people,
wise to listen to virtue,
and enlightened to achieve far-reaching goals.'
Moreover, the *Shī* describes the virtue of King Wén,
saying:
'Only this King Wén,
God measured his heart,
and stilled his virtuous fame.
His virtue could shine brightly,
shining brightly and setting an example;
he could lead and he could rule,
king over this great state.
He could be gentle and he could be kind,
kind like King Wén,
his virtue without regret.
Having received God's blessings,
he extends them to his descendants.'
'The heart able to control righteousness is called "measure";'
'virtuous governance responding in harmony is called "still";'
'illuminating and overseeing the four directions is called "bright";'
'exerting effort without selfishness is called "example";'
'teaching tirelessly is called "leadership";'
'rewarding and punishing with authority is called "rule";'
'kindness and harmony universally accepted is called "gentleness";'
'choosing the good and following it is called "kindness";'
'ordering heaven and earth is called "culture."'
These constitute the nine virtues of beauty.
What need is there to esteem mere skills and arts?
Now, suppose a ruler's vision were as keen as Lílóu's,
his hearing as acute as Shī Kuàng's,
his charioteering as skilled as Wáng Liáng's,
his archery as masterful as Yí Yì's,
his calligraphy as refined as Shǐ Zhòu's,
his calculation as precise as Lì Shǒu's,
his running could overtake a team of four horses,
his strength could break a door bolt—
possessing these six abilities,
he could be called excellent in the duties of an official.
But what benefit would this bring to governance?
Lacking these six abilities,
he could be called deficient in the duties of an official,
but what increase would this bring to disorder?
It must be because they abandon benevolence and righteousness and hinder the Way and virtue.
Why is this?
A small vessel cannot hold everything.
Since order and chaos do not depend on these,
yet they are what men of mediocre talent delight in.
In the past, Lù Fēngshū and the downfall of Jìn's Zhì Bóyáo
both relied on their three talents,
depended on their five virtues,
yet perished because of their lack of benevolence.
Therefore, if a ruler possesses many skills,
delights in petty cleverness,
but does not comprehend the great principles,
it is precisely enough to reject the advice of remonstrators and silence the mouths of the loyal and upright.
It is merely enough to follow the traces of perished states
and turn away from the path that secures the family.
Is this not so?
Is this not so?
The emperor rises at dawn to oversee the court,
faces south to administer the realm—
with whom will he accomplish this?
Is it not with the multitude of dukes, ministers, and officers!
Therefore, great ministers must be the right men.
Great ministers are the ruler's limbs and ears, his eyes,
through which he sees and hears,
through which he acts.
The former kings knew it was thus,
therefore they broadly sought wise, intelligent, and profound gentlemen,
placed them in high positions,
and entrusted them with the state's governance and decrees.
If those who govern are intelligent and wise,
then their affairs succeed;
if their affairs succeed,
then all officials will not fail in their duties;
if all officials do not fail in their duties,
then all matters will not fail to achieve order;
if all matters achieve order,
then the people of the nine regions will all find their proper place.
Therefore, the *Book of Documents* says:
"If the head is enlightened,
and the limbs are good,
then all affairs are prosperous."
Thus, great ministers are the vital instruments for governing the myriad states,
they cannot be established by public praise.
The ruler should personally examine them;
public praise can only bring a man to his notice.
Thus, when Yáo heard of Shùn,
it was through public praise;
but when he appointed him,
it was through what his own mind perceived.
There are also cases where a great worthy is obtained not through public praise.
Was this not King Wén!
Hunting by the banks of the Wèi River,
he met on the road Jiāng Tàigōng,
white-haired and hoary,
just then holding a rod and fishing.
King Wén summoned him and spoke with him,
and he was a fitting assistant for an emperor or king.
So he took him back in his carriage,
and made him Grand Tutor.
Jiāng Tàigōng at that time was poor and lowly,
and moreover old in years;
there was no recommendation from the noble and prominent.
His words truly matched the heart of a worthy ruler,
his methods truly accorded with the way to achieve peace.
King Wén's discernment
was brilliantly clear, as if parting clouds to see the sun;
suddenly bright, as if opening mist to behold the sky.
How could this have been borrowed from the multitude!
Not only sages are like this,
but even hegemons also have such discernment.
In the past, Duke Huán of Qí went out early in the morning.
Nìng Qì was then a traveler,
sleeping beneath a large cart.
He struck an ox horn and sang.
His song was sorrowful and stirring,
its lyrics expressing grievances against the world.
Duke Huán knew he was no ordinary man.
He summoned him and spoke with him,
and he turned out to be a man capable of achieving great deeds.
Thereupon, he promoted and employed him,
entrusting him with the governance of the state.
Whenever an enlightened ruler employs people,
he never fails to understand them through his own insight,
nor does he blindly rely on public praise.
To employ people based solely on public praise
is not to desire good governance,
but to seek fame.
Thus, if one does not perceive things for oneself
but instead uses public praise as the standard,
this is what is called "conforming to public praise,"
not what is called "obtaining the worthy and capable."
If one were to consider public praise as the measure of worthiness and capability,
then Bó Gǔn would not have faced the calamity at Yǔshān,
and Táng Yú would not have incurred the nine-year expense.
Sages know that public praise may be right or wrong,
so when they employ people,
they sometimes rely on it and sometimes act independently,
not using a single criterion.
Moreover, those making recommendations are not the Four Peaks,
and the age is not that of Táng Yú.
The Great Way has fallen into obscurity,
and perverse doctrines prevail.
Ministers are already deceitful,
and the people are already confused.
Without the clarity of independent insight,
relying solely on the praise of the masses,
without personal scrutiny,
without examination of affairs,
how can one obtain great worthies?
Moreover, great worthies dwell in humble alleys,
and are certainly not recognized by the vulgar crowd.
Why is this?
Great worthies in their conduct
are humble and do not display themselves,
appearing simple as if incapable.
They do not contend with the times over right and wrong,
nor debate with the vulgar over straight and crooked.
They do not boast of fame,
do not shun slander,
and do not seek praise.
Their flavor is utterly bland,
their appearance utterly plain.
Being thus,
how do they differ from ordinary people?
Where they differ from ordinary people
is that their minds govern all principles without error,
their wisdom encompasses all things without excess,
they remain unperturbed when sudden changes occur,
and they are not misled when truth and falsehood abound.
Thus, when they achieve their aims, the state is governed with harmony,
the altars of soil and grain are secure and firm,
the myriad people receive their blessings,
and all living beings rely on their grace.
Within the eight extremes, all become one.
This is truly not something the vulgar crowd can foresee.
Otherwise,
how could they gain resounding fame?
That resounding fame
is all shaped by the vulgar crowd's perspective,
and distorted to align with the vulgar crowd's hearing.
The noble person is certainly not like this.
In the past, Guǎn Yíwú fought three battles and was defeated each time.
People all said he lacked courage.
When sharing wealth with others,
he took more,
and people all said he was not honest.
He did not die for the calamity of Zǐ Jiū,
and people all said he betrayed righteousness.
If at that time there had been no recommendation from Bào Shū
and no hearing from the hegemonic ruler,
his splendid achievements would not have been established in the world,
and his great name would not have been passed down to later generations.
He would have remained a lowly man forever.
The people of Lǔ saw that Zhòngní was fond of yielding and did not contend,
and they also said he was incapable.
They made a song about him:
"Plain boots and lamb fur robe,
seeking him brings no blame.
Lamb fur robe and plain boots,
seeking him brings no fault."
With the virtue of a sage,
bright and illustrious,
lofty, vast, broad, and profound,
he should have been easily understood.
Yet even he was like this—
how much more so for the worthy?
From this we may argue
that those not praised by contemporary customs
are not necessarily wrong.
And those who are praised
are not necessarily right.
Thus, the *Book of Songs* says:
"On the mountain grows the fusu tree,
in the marsh blooms the lotus flower.
I do not see the handsome Zǐdū,
but instead encounter a madman."
This means that what is called beautiful is not beautiful,
and what is called ugly is not ugly.
This is also due to the disorder of the times.
In a well-governed age, it is not so.
The rulers of a declining age are born in chaos.
When seeking great ministers and appointing prime ministers, they believe the talk of the vulgar crowd.
Thus, they cannot avoid the ridicule of the *Guófēng*.
And if they wish with such ministers to promote heavenly harmony,
achieve timely peace,
halt calamities and chaos,
and quell disasters and anomalies,
it is no different from riding a horse with worn-out hooves
and ascending the perilous Tàiháng Mountains—
they are sure to stumble and fall.
Thus, the *Book of Documents* says:
"The arms and legs are ruined,
and all affairs collapse."
This is what it means.
Thus, the noble person is not praised by contemporary customs.
If we speak of praise for filial piety, fraternal duty, loyalty, and trustworthiness,
then there is such praise.
But praise for governing the state and achieving peace—
this has never existed.
Their praise is no greater than that given to scholars versed in exegesis.
The methods for governing the state and achieving peace
cannot be mastered by just anyone;
they cannot be mutually understood without the right person.
Such persons are few,
and the few cannot match the many.
Who, then, will be able to distinguish them?
Thus, if the noble person does not meet with his time,
he will not be as renowned and illustrious as the vulgar scholars.
Not only that,
he will also be judged and constrained by the vulgar scholars.
Distinctions of high and low,
prices of noble and base,
all come from their mouths.
Thus, even after a lifetime of effort,
he cannot avoid being a common man.
In the past, Xún Qing lived during the Warring States period.
He possessed profound and wise talent,
traced back to Yáo and Shùn,
modeled himself on Wén and Wǔ,
and revered Zhòngní as his master.
He clarified the way to quell chaos,
yet the rulers of the various states considered him impractical,
not understanding the changes of the times,
and in the end, none were willing to employ him.
As for the itinerant persuaders,
though their methods were perverse,
they led their followers,
and their names shook the feudal lords.
In every state they went to,
none failed to receive them with full ceremony outside the city,
sweeping the path ahead with brooms,
and granting them titles and rewards as honored guests—
such instances were too numerous to count.
Thus, the mismatch between name and reality
has existed for a long time.
In which age has it not existed?
Only when the world possesses the Way
will such things be abolished.
What people often say is:
"Enlightened rulers set aside themselves and follow others,
thus their states are governed and secure.
Foolish rulers oppose others and act on their own,
thus their states fall into chaos and danger."
This is a one-sided, biased view,
not the ultimate discourse of the Great Way.
The distinction between security and danger,
order and chaos,
lies in knowing whom to follow,
not in necessarily following others.
All rulers have those they follow,
yet some face danger and insecurity—
this is because they follow the wrong ones.
All rulers have those they oppose,
yet some achieve order without chaos—
this is because they oppose the right ones.
Now, the wise rulers personally employ
those who are upright, good, intelligent, and wise;
their words
are all about virtue, righteousness, loyalty, and trustworthiness.
Thus, following them leads to stability,
while not following them leads to peril.
The foolish rulers personally employ
those who are flattering, wicked, foolish, and deluded;
their words
are all about treachery, deceit, and sycophancy.
How can following them bring order,
and how can not following them bring chaos?
In the past, Duke Huán of Qí followed Guǎn Zhòng and achieved stability;
the Second Emperor followed Zhào Gāo and faced peril.
Emperor Shùn rejected the Four Villains and brought order;
King Zhòu of Yīn rejected the Three Benevolent Men and brought chaos.
Thus, not knowing whom to follow yet eagerly following others,
or not knowing whom to reject yet eagerly rejecting others—
their failures are the same.
Confucius said:
"Knowing what cannot be followed,
one then knows what can be followed."
Now, words may appear correct yet be false in reality;
they may appear beautiful yet ruin affairs;
they may appear compliant yet violate the Way.
These three types cannot be discerned except by the most enlightened rulers.
King Zhāo of Yān sent Yuè Yì to attack Qí,
capturing over seventy cities,
with Jǔ and Jímò not yet taken.
When King Zhāo died,
King Huì, who had been the crown prince,
had previously been at odds with Yì.
Tián Dān, the defender of Jímò,
spread disinformation in Yān,
causing rumors to say:
"The king is already dead,
and only three cities remain untaken."
Yuè Yì, having a rift with the new king,
feared execution and dared not return.
Outwardly, he used attacking Qí as a pretext,
but in reality, he intended to take advantage of the Qí people's lack of allegiance,
thus delaying the capture of Jímò to await developments.
What the Qí people feared
was only that another general would come,
for then Jímò would be destroyed.
King Huì believed this to be true,
sent Qí Jié to replace him,
and was greatly defeated by Tián Dān.
This is an example of words appearing correct yet being false in reality.
The Yān minister Zǐ Zhī was favored by the king
and wished to monopolize state power.
Someone spoke to King Kuài of Yān on his behalf, saying:
"People say Yáo was a worthy ruler
because he yielded the empire to Xǔ Yóu.
Xǔ Yóu did not accept it,
so Yáo gained the reputation of yielding the empire,
yet in reality did not lose it.
If Your Majesty now yields the state to Minister Zǐ Zhī,
Zǐ Zhī will certainly not dare accept it.
Thus, you will be acting in the same manner as Yáo."
King Kuài of Yān followed this advice,
and his state fell into great chaos.
This is an example of words appearing beautiful yet ruining affairs.
Duke Jǐng of Qí wished to depose Crown Prince Yángshēng
and establish his illegitimate son Tú instead.
He said to the senior official Chén Qǐ:
"I wish to establish Tú.
What do you think?"
Qǐ replied:
"What pleases one about being a ruler
is that if you wish to establish someone, you establish them;
if you do not wish to establish someone, you do not.
If Your Lordship wishes to establish him,
then your servant requests to establish him."
Thus, Tú was established.
This is an example of words appearing compliant yet violating the Way.
Moreover, words are spoken and implemented in the present moment,
but their effects appear in later days.
The later days arrive slowly,
while the present moment requires swift decisions.
Thus, the clever often prevail,
while the clumsy often fail—
such is the natural tendency.
This describes the listening of a mediocre ruler.
As for a foolish ruler,
he does not examine whether the words are clever or clumsy.
Two strategies are presented together,
and he follows the one that fulfills his own desires.
A wise ruler does not examine whether the words are clever or clumsy either.
Two strategies are presented together,
and he follows the one that brings him benefit.
Thus, Emperor Gāozǔ and Emperor Guāngwǔ
were able to gather the strengths of all strategies
and discard their weaknesses,
thereby gaining all within the Four Seas
and establishing the title of Emperor.
King Fūchāi of Wú, King Huái of Chǔ, and King Xiāng of Chǔ
discarded the excellent plans of Wǔ Yuán and Qū Yuán,
and adopted the flattering words of Pǐ and Shàngguān,
thereby losing the lands of Jiāng and Hàn
and forfeiting the ancestral temples' sovereignty.
These two emperors and three kings
also followed others at times,
and rejected others at times.
Yet their success and failure diverged sharply, their rise and fall followed different paths—
it was a matter of recognizing strategies or failing to recognize them.
Not knowing whom to follow is very easy,
but recognizing strategies is very difficult.
Examining the evidence impartially,
this is indeed the case.
A question is asked:
"All people love life and hate death,
love pleasure and hate sorrow.
Yet observing their actions,
some abandon life and embrace death,
some abandon pleasure and embrace sorrow.
Do their likes and dislikes differ from others'?"
The reply:
"It is not that their likes and dislikes differ from others',
but rather that their methods of seeking life and pleasure have lost the proper way.
It is like a lost person wishing to go south but heading north instead.
Now, let me briefly cite one example to illustrate.
In the past, after Xiàng Yǔ was defeated
and pursued by Hàn troops,
he said to his remaining cavalry:
'I have raised troops for eight years now,
personally experienced over seventy battles,
defeated all I attacked,
and thus dominated the world.
Now I am trapped here—
this is Heaven destroying me,
not a fault of my warfare.'
This is all a case of desiring south but heading north regarding survival and demise.
Now, warfare and battle are minor matters for a true king—
they are not the means to gain the world.
For a true king to gain the world,
there is a great foundation,
which is called benevolence and wisdom.
With benevolence, all states cherish him;
with wisdom, all heroes submit to him.
Governing all states,
commanding all heroes,
and overseeing the Four Seas—
who could contend with him?
As for attacking cities that must be taken,
and winning every field battle—
these are matters for generals and commanders.
Xiàng Yǔ, with the capacity of a petty man,
was ignorant of the teachings for emperors and kings.
He thought gaining the world relied solely on warfare.
He boasted of his courage and strength,
practiced deceit and cruelty without affection,
was greedy, stingy, and monopolized profits,
did not reward merit and diligence,
had one Fàn Zēng,
yet could not employ him,
and instead grew suspicious of him,
until Fàn Zēng, filled with indignation and heartbreak,
died from a festering boil.
Heroes rebelled and betrayed him,
strategists left and deserted him,
leading to his dire straits,
and he himself was captured.
Yet he still did not understand why he had lost,
instead glaring fiercely and breaking through encirclements,
beheading generals and capturing banners,
to prove it was not a fault of his warfare.
How profoundly mistaken he was!
Emperor Gāozǔ enumerated his ten crimes—
that was merely a general outline.
As for minor faults and errors,
unknown to the world,
how could they all be counted?
Moreover, while a chaotic ruler has not yet perished,
no one dares to remonstrate with him;
and after he perishes,
no one can fully investigate him.
Thus, he remains unenlightened until death—
is this truly so strange?"
Generally, in the case of rulers who lose their states,
their courts are never without ministers capable of bringing order,
and their treasuries are never without the books of former kings.
Yet they cannot avoid destruction—
why is this?
It is because their worthies are not employed,
and their laws are not implemented.
If laws are written but not put into practice,
and worthies are enfeoffed but their ways are not followed,
then laws are no different from roadside talk,
and worthies are no different from wooden spirit tablets.
In the past, Jié fled to Náncháo,
Zhòu fell at the capital,
Lì was exiled to Zhì,
Yōu perished at Xì.
At that time,
the laws of the three sage-kings still existed,
and ministers of good counsel still remained.
Moving down to the Spring and Autumn period,
Chǔ had Wǔ Jǔ, Zuǒshǐ Yǐxiāng, Yòuyǐn Zǐgé, and Báigōng Zǐzhāng,
yet King Líng lost his army;
Wèi had Tàishū Yí, Gōngzǐ Zhuān, Qú Bóyù, and Shǐ Qiū,
yet Duke Xiàn fled into exile;
Jìn had Zhào Xuānmèng, Fàn Wǔzǐ, and Grand Scribe Dǒng Hú,
yet Duke Líng was assassinated;
Lǔ had Zǐjiā Jī and Shūsūn Ruò,
yet Duke Zhāo died in the wilderness;
Qí had Yàn Píngzhòng and Nánshǐshì,
yet Duke Zhuāng could not avoid being murdered;
Yú and Guó had Gōng Zhīqí and Zhōu Zhīqiáo,
yet the two lords lost their ancestral sacrifices.
From this we can see,
if worthy men are not employed,
even having them is of no benefit.
Yet these several states,
all had worthy men who were former ministers of earlier rulers or hereditary officials,
not sought from afar.
There were also those who sought from afar yet did not employ them.
In the past, Duke Huán of Qí established the Jìxià Academy,
created the title of Grand Master,
to attract worthy men and honor them.
From Mèng Kē's disciples onward, all traveled to Qí;
Lord Chūnshēn of Chǔ also favored guests,
respectfully treated heroes,
gathering talents from all directions,
his retainers filled the halls,
and he even hired Xún Qīng,
placing him in Lánlíng.
Yet Qí did not become stronger,
Huáng Xiē met with disaster,
because they were not employed.
Seeking worthy men from afar yet not employing them—
why is this?
The nature of a worthy man
is not like beautiful consorts and lovely concubines who are pleasing to the eye;
nor like ceremonial caps and robes that can be worn on the body;
nor like fine delicacies and various dishes that can fill the mouth.
They are to be used for their counsel,
if their counsel is not used,
what is the use of having many?
If one merely wants to fill the roster of officials,
without inquiring into the substance of their virtue,
then it would be better to cast golden statues,
and array them at court.
Moreover, there would be no expense of salaries.
Yet they also know that having horses requires riding them to travel far,
having doctors requires employing them to cure illness.
But when it comes to having worthy men,
they do not understand they must be employed to bring about good governance—
why is this?
Are worthy men difficult to recognize?
Then why seek them from afar?
Are they easy to recognize?
Then why not employ them?
Is it because there are too few, insufficient for use, and one must first increase their number?
This is even more deluded.
A worthy man is praised by others,
not for his strength;
strength requires many,
but wisdom does not require a multitude.
Thus a king's army numbers seventy thousand,
but his assistants are the six ministers.
Thus Shùn had five ministers and the world was well-governed,
Zhōu had ten able ministers and all within the four seas submitted,
is this not proof that few are sufficient?
Moreover, the rulers of the six states,
though they did not employ the worthy,
when they attracted men,
still cultivated ritual and showed full sincerity,
not daring to insult or slight them.
As for Wáng Mǎng,
he could not employ them,
and when he attracted them,
he could not even speak properly.
Wáng Mǎng's character
was inwardly treacherous and evil,
outwardly admiring ancient righteousness,
he also hired famous Confucian scholars,
summoned masters of arts,
but his governance was oppressive, his teachings cruel,
unable to truly attract them.
Thus he coerced them with harsh punishments,
intimidated them with severe executions,
the worthy were fearful,
none dared not come.
He merely set up empty reputations to boast throughout the land.
Mǎng also ultimately perished.
Moreover, when Mǎng enfeoffed men,
he in fact imprisoned them.
To imprison someone does not necessarily mean putting them in shackles
and placing them in a jail;
it means to constrain and confine them, to cause them worry and sorrow.
He made it so that those at court, if they wished to advance, could not present their plans;
if they wished to withdraw, could not find peace for themselves.
This is to use silk ribbons as ropes,
and seals and pendants as fetters and manacles.
Petty men may delight in this,
but noble men consider it disgraceful.
Therefore, when an enlightened ruler obtains worthy men,
he wins their hearts,
not merely their persons.
If he obtains their persons
but does not consider their hearts,
this is no different from caging birds or penning beasts.
Then the worthy man, to me,
is like an enemy,
how could he be of use to me?
Even if I say:
"I bestow a salary of ten thousand zhōng."
What good would it do?
Thus, if you win their hearts,
even ten thousand lǐ is near;
if you lose their hearts,
sharing the same quilt is distant.
Now, if one does not cultivate what wins the hearts of the worthy,
but instead insists on methods that merely control their persons,
until the altars of soil and grain are overturned,
and the ancestral temples are destroyed and cut off,
is this not lamentable?
Xúnzǐ said:
"The trouble with a ruler
lies not in saying he does not employ the worthy,
but in truly not employing them."
To speak of employing the worthy is the mouth,
to reject the worthy is action.
When mouth and action are contrary,
and one desires the worthy to advance,
and the unworthy to withdraw,
is that not difficult indeed!
Those who catch cicadas by torchlight must ensure their fire is bright and shake the tree—that is all.
If the fire is not bright,
even shaking the tree is of no use.
If a ruler is capable of making his virtue shine,
then the world will turn to him as cicadas are drawn to the fire.
How well said!
In the past, Yī Yǐn was in the fields,
delighting in the ways of Yáo and Shùn.
Hearing that Chéng Tāng was rising,
he went from the Xià to the Shāng.
Tài Gōng, avoiding the wickedness of Zhòu,
dwelt by the shores of the Eastern Sea.
Hearing that King Wén was rising,
he also went from the Shāng to the Zhōu.
Next, Nìng Qì went to Qí,
Bǎilǐ Xī entered Qín,
Fàn Lǐ went to Yuè,
and Yuè Yì traveled to Yān.
Therefore, if a ruler cultivates his moral principles,
makes his virtuous reputation illustrious,
is careful with his dignified demeanor,
scrutinizes his edicts and commands,
ensures punishments are not biased or perverse,
and there are no wrongful imprisonments or cruel penalties,
if his benevolence and love are widespread and sincere,
and his kindness and favor flow far and wide,
if all officials delight in their duties,
and the myriad people find their proper place,
then the worthy will look up to him as to heaven and earth,
love him as their own kin,
rejoice in him as in the harmony of xūn and chí flutes,
and savor him as the fragrance of orchids.
Thus, when they come to me,
it is like breaking a dam to guide stagnant water into a great ravine—
how could they not arrive?
But if he is crude, filthy, violent, and cruel,
with no fragrance of virtue rising,
slanderers and evil men at his side,
flatterers and sycophants filling the court,
killing the innocent,
punishments excessive and harmful,
palaces lofty and extravagant,
wives and concubines without restraint,
bells struck and dancing girls entertained,
debauchery and pleasure indulged daily,
taxes numerous and heavy,
resources and strength exhausted,
the people freezing and starving,
corpses of the dead filling the wilds,
arrogant and self-satisfied,
advisors being executed,
inside and outside shaken with fear,
far and near filled with resentment and sorrow—
then when the worthy look upon my appearance,
it seems like a demon;
my towers and halls,
like a prison;
my embroidered robes,
like mourning clothes;
the music of strings and songs,
like wailing and crying;
fine wines,
like filthy water;
delicacies and feasts,
like dung and dirt;
every action and measure taken,
lacks a single good.
If they detest me like this,
how would they be willing to come?
Now, if one does not strive to make his righteousness clear,
but merely sets out emoluments and salaries,
he may attract petty men,
but will find it hard to gain gentlemen.
A gentleman acts without compromising to fit in,
stands firm without changing his direction;
he does not distort the Way for the sake of the world,
nor harm benevolence for the sake of preserving his life.
How can he be lured by salary?
Even if forced and seized, he will not be won over.
He will merely shut his mouth and feign foolishness,
barely avoiding harm, with no leisure for service.
On what then will the safety of the state rely?
Therefore, the *Book of Songs* says:
"Dignified demeanor is all lost,
good men become like corpses."
This is what it means.
There are two great guiding principles of governance.
What are these two?
They are called rewards and punishments.
If a ruler understands the way of rewards and punishments,
then orderly rule is not difficult.
Rewards and punishments do not necessarily lie in being severe,
but in being carried out consistently.
If consistently carried out, then even if not severe, the people will be respectful.
If not consistently carried out, then even if severe, the people will become negligent.
Therefore, the former kings strove to ensure rewards and punishments were consistently applied.
The *Book of Documents* says:
"If you have no disbelief,
I will not go back on my word.
If you do not follow the oath,
I will put you and your children to death,
with no pardon."
"Heaven gave birth to the multitudes of people,"
their nature is one.
Cutting flesh and injuring the body—
all detest it.
Wearing embroidered robes and adorned with elegance—
all desire it.
These two things constantly exist,
yet the people do not govern themselves.
There is a reason for this.
Those who should be rewarded are not rewarded;
those who should be punished are not punished.
When those who should be rewarded are not rewarded,
then those who do good lose their fundamental hope
and doubt their own actions.
When those who should be punished are not punished,
then those who do evil regard the state's laws lightly
and persist in their conduct.
If it is like this,
even if axes are used daily in the marketplace,
the people will not abandon evil.
Even if titles and salaries are bestowed daily at court,
the people will not be inspired to do good.
Therefore, the sage does not dare to abolish punishments due to the affection for relatives,
nor dare to abolish rewards due to resentment toward enemies.
Why is this?
It is to provide a remedy.
Thus, the *Sīmǎ Fǎ* says:
"Rewards and punishments should not be delayed,
so that the people may quickly see the recompense for good and evil."
Delay is still unacceptable,
how much more so abolishing them?
Rewards and punishments should not be too sparse,
nor too frequent.
If too frequent, those affected become many;
if too sparse, those overlooked become many.
Rewards and punishments should not be too heavy,
nor too light.
If rewards are too light, the people are not encouraged;
if punishments are too light, the people have no fear.
If rewards are too heavy, the people become opportunistic;
if punishments are too heavy, the people are left without hope.
Therefore, the former kings, with clear understanding and forbearance, administered them,
seeking the mean to achieve fairness,
without losing proper measure.
Thus, the *Book of Documents* says:
"All is in the mean;
examine the words for discrepancies."
Rewards and punishments for the myriad people
are like reins and whip for a team of four horses.
If the reins and whip are not well-adjusted,
it is not merely a matter of speed,
but may lead to overturning the carriage and breaking the axle.
If rewards and punishments are not clear,
it is not merely a distinction between order and chaos,
but may lead to the destruction of the state and loss of life.
Can one not be cautious?
Can one not be cautious?
Therefore, the *Book of Songs* says:
"Holding the reins as if weaving silk,
the two side horses dance."
This speaks of how good driving can be applied to governing the state.
Order and peace lie in the flourishing of all tasks;
the flourishing of all tasks lies in the equitable distribution of labor;
the equitable distribution of labor lies in the thorough accounting of the population;
the thorough accounting of the population is the foundation of the state.
Therefore, the former kings thoroughly knew the numbers of their myriad people,
and then divided them into nine occupations.
Once the nine occupations were divided,
the diligent could be seen,
and the lazy could be heard of.
Under such circumstances, inequitable distribution of labor
has never occurred.
Once labor is equitably distributed,
the people give their full hearts and exhaust their strength.
Under such circumstances, the non-flourishing of all tasks
has never occurred.
Once all tasks flourish,
the state becomes prosperous and wealthy,
great and small lacking nothing,
the people content and harmonious,
with no resentment or grievance below.
Under such circumstances, disorder and lack of peace
has never occurred.
Therefore it is said:
Water has a source,
governance has a root.
The Way lies in examining this root, that is all.
The *Zhōu Lǐ* states:
"In the first month of winter, the Minister of Justice presents the population figures to the king.
The king bows and receives them,
depositing them in the heavenly archive.
The Inner Scribe, the Accountant, and the Prime Minister keep duplicate records."
Such is the importance placed on this.
In ancient times, the sage kings established rituals and laws,
so that the noble had constant dignity,
and the lowly had distinct gradations.
The gentlemen and the common people
each attended to their proper duties;
thus, those below did not transgress against those above,
and human labor and material resources
could mutually supply and suffice.
In the past, wealthy people across the land, as well as merchants and artisans,
possessed immense fortunes,
and employed male and female servants,
some numbering in the hundreds,
others in the tens.
How could this have been the intention of the former kings in establishing rituals!
Now, the state has four classes of people,
who should not interfere with or encroach upon each other:
the scholars exert their minds,
while the artisans, farmers, and merchants exert their strength.
"Those who exert their minds are called gentlemen;
those who exert their strength are called common people.
The gentlemen govern others;
the common people are governed by others.
Those who are governed by others feed others;
those who govern others are fed by others.
This is the universal principle of all kings."
Now, those among the people who possess wealth without virtue
should be governed by others and feed others,
yet they employ male and female servants,
do not toil their sinews and strength,
but merely gesture with their eyes and chin,
composed and idle,
while even those who cherish loyalty and trustworthiness,
read the books of sages and wise men,
dress properly and hold the tablet,
and stand in court positions—
how can they surpass this?
Moreover, many gentlemen today
are still impoverished and lacking,
with no male or female servants at home.
Even if they have some,
they are insufficient to serve their needs,
so their wives and children toil diligently,
and they themselves cook the meals.
What is the reason for this?
It is all because profit-seekers compete with them,
and there are also those families who wear purple and blue sashes and engage in monopolies that cause this.
When things have excess,
they also have deficiency.
The sages knew it was so,
therefore they took from the surplus to supplement the deficit,
weighed things and distributed them evenly,
acting to guard against excess,
not allowing it to go beyond measure.
Thus, good governance could be achieved.
To govern a state and cause gentlemen of integrity and humility to be so lacking,
while allowing the greedy to have such abundance,
is not the way to distinguish between noble and lowly, grade the esteemed and humble, devalue wealth and profit, and uphold virtue and morality.
Now, the reason why commandery governors and county magistrates can be called "lord"
is because rewards, punishments, and authority
all issue from themselves.
If the people keep male and female servants,
some even up to several hundred,
and rewards, punishments, and authority
also issue from themselves,
then how are they different from the commandery and county officials?
Though male and female servants are lowly,
they all possess the five constant virtues;
they are originally the good people of the emperor,
yet they are made to serve the registered common people,
pitifully destitute and displaced,
with nowhere to appeal—
is this not unjust?
Now, from the minor clerks and assistants and above,
up to the feudal lords and kings,
all are those who govern the people;
they should be allowed to keep male and female servants.
Farmers, artisans, merchants, and those who run errands and serve,
all are those who toil with their strength and are governed by others;
they should not be allowed to keep them.
In the past, when Emperor Āi of Hàn ascended the throne,
Shī Dān assisted in governance
and proposed that limits be set on those who kept fields, houses, and male and female servants.
At that time, the Dīng and Fù families were in power,
and Dǒng Xián was favored and honored;
they were all displeased with this,
so the matter was abandoned.
Shī Dān and his like
were all renowned ministers of the previous court,
who were concerned about monopolistic families,
submitted loyal and trustworthy proposals,
and established prohibitions for the state.
Yet they were suppressed by treacherous ministers,
and ultimately their proposals were not implemented.
How much more so for common scholars in plain cloth,
who wish to advocate and establish regulations—
is that not far-fetched!
